titles.en: Ten things to know before your first orbital flight

descriptions.en: The six-hour shuttle from Port Kestrel to Halcyon is routine, but your first one won't feel it. A former launch-pad hostel keeper on ears, stomachs, water, sleep and that first view.

bodies.en:
For years I ran a hostel so close to the Port Kestrel launch pads that the windows hummed before every departure, and most mornings I watched a few first-time flyers push their breakfast round the plate. The shuttle up to Halcyon Station is the most routine journey in the Reach. It is also, the first time, the strangest six hours of most people's lives. Here is what I wish I had told every one of them.

Six hours in three acts

The flight divides neatly. First comes the climb: a few minutes in which the engines press you into your seat at about three times your weight. Then the long coast, when you are weightless and the cabin becomes something between a waiting room and an aquarium. Last comes the docking at Halcyon's hub and the ride out to the Rim, where your weight comes back. None of it is dangerous for a healthy traveller. What follows is about comfort, not survival.

The ten things

  1. Eat lightly, but eat. A plain meal two or three hours before boarding is ideal: bread, rice, a bowl of noodles from an Old Docks counter without the chilli. An empty stomach is no protection against queasiness, and a heavy one is a liability once things start floating. Skip fizzy drinks. Bubbles do not behave in weightlessness, and nor will you.
  2. Dress for a long-haul liner, not a party. Wear soft layers with no belt buckles or hard seams across the back, because you will spend the climb pressed into the seat. Bring socks with grip: shoes come off and are stowed. Anything loose, from scarves to lanyards to long earrings, will drift into your face or your neighbour's. Tie long hair back.
  3. The climb is short, and it is heavy. For a few minutes you will weigh about three times what you do on Calder. It feels like a large, friendly dog lying on your chest. Keep your head back against the rest, breathe from your belly and do not try to lift your arms for a picture. The window shows little but sky turning from blue to black.
  4. Look after your ears. The cabin pressure is adjusted on the way up, and some people feel it as they would on an aircraft coming in to land. Swallow, yawn or chew; the crew hand out sweets for exactly this reason. If you have a cold, take a decongestant before boarding and mention it at check-in.
  5. Your stomach will notice the silence. When the engines cut, the weight simply stops, and for many people the first sensation is of falling. That is accurate: you are falling around Calder, and you will keep doing so until you dock. Perhaps a third of first-timers feel unwell for a while. Keep your head still, fix your eyes on something inside the cabin rather than the window, and use the bag in the seat pocket without embarrassment. Motion-sickness tablets taken an hour before boarding help most people.
  6. Drink little and often. In weightlessness the fluid in your body drifts upward, your face puffs and your sense of thirst becomes unreliable. Sip from the valve pouch you are given, and do not save it all for the end. The toilets work, but they come with a briefing, and you would rather not need one in the first hour.
  7. Move slowly, with your fingertips. When the belt sign goes off you may float free. The trick is to push off gently and stop yourself with fingertips, not shoulders. Everything you push against pushes back, so a firm shove sends you across the cabin far faster than you meant. Crews tell people to move like a slow swimmer in a crowded pool, and it is good advice.
  8. Sleep if you can. The coast lasts several hours and the cabin lights stay low for most of it. Strap in loosely, pull your hood up or use the eyeshade provided, and let your arms float. They will rise in front of you like a sleepwalker's, which is normal. People who doze on the way up arrive far better company than people who watched every minute.
  9. Save some attention for the first view. Somewhere in the second hour the window blinds go up. Calder's curve fills the glass, its atmosphere a thin blue line along the edge, and if the timing is right you will see a sunrise break across it in a band of red. Nothing prepares you for how thin that blue line is. Let the photographers have the window first, then take your time.
  10. Arriving is a gentle surprise. You dock at Halcyon's hub, which barely seems to turn, so you leave the shuttle still weightless, pulling yourself along handrails. Then a lift carries you down one of the spokes and your weight returns as you go: a little at first, then most of it. By the Rim deck you weigh nearly what you did on Calder, because the great wheel, 2.4 km across, turns once every 70 seconds. Your legs will feel odd for an hour. Walk slowly and find a seat by a window.

My best advice is also the dullest: tell the crew it is your first flight. They will seat you away from the galley, check on you after the engines cut and warn you before the sunrise arrives. They have flown thousands of first-timers, and you will not be the most nervous one aboard.

Before you leave the Kestrel

Check-in at the shuttle halls closes an hour before departure, and you should be there well before that. Security is thorough, and the medical questionnaire asks about recent colds, ear trouble and your heart. Hand luggage is limited to one soft bag that fits under the seat in front; hard cases go in the hold, and anything with a battery must be declared.

If you are spending the night before in Port Kestrel, stay close to the halls. The Old Docks hostels are a short walk away, and the early departures are the ones most likely to leave on time. Go to bed early, set two alarms and skip the last round at the night market.

The shuttle at a glance

  • Port Kestrel to Halcyon Station: about 6 hours
  • The climb: a few minutes at about three times your weight
  • Then weightless until docking at the hub
  • Check-in closes 60 minutes before departure
  • Hand luggage: one soft bag that fits under the seat
  • On the Rim deck: nearly your full Calder weight

The second time

Every regular traveller I know remembers their first flight in detail and the next twenty hardly at all. By the second trip you will have a routine: the plain breakfast, the sweets for your ears, a nap through the coast. Soon you will be the one telling a nervous stranger to breathe from the belly. Until then, enjoy the strangeness. It does not last.

titles.en: The Lantern, explained: what you are actually looking at

descriptions.en: A pale smudge to the eye, a blaze of green and red in Brightwater's infrared pictures. What the Lantern nebula is, what its false colours mean and where in the Reach to see it yourself.

bodies.en:
Ask anyone who has stood on Veyra's dark side what the Lantern looks like and you will get two answers. The first, honest one: a pale smudge, wider than your outstretched hand, that you are never entirely sure you are seeing. The second comes held out on a screen: a burst of green, red and blue, threaded with dark lanes and studded with bright knots. Both are true. The distance between them is the whole story of the Lantern.

A cloud lit from within

The Lantern is a nebula, an enormous cloud of gas and dust far beyond the outermost world of the Reach. It is so far away that the light reaching your eye tonight set out long before anyone lived on Calder. Most of the cloud is hydrogen, cold and dark. What makes it shine is the young stars embedded inside it: hot, heavy and fierce, burning through their fuel at a rate that Ilyr, a calm middle-aged star, would find reckless.

Their light does two things. It warms the dust around them until the dust glows with heat, the way a stone left in the sun is warm to the touch after dark. And it tears electrons from the gas, which then gives off light of its own as they are recaptured, the trick behind a lit shop sign. The Lantern is not lit from outside, like a cloud at sunset. It is a lamp with its own flames inside.

Some of those flames are still being lit. In the region called the Nursery, dense knots of gas are collapsing under their own weight, warming as they shrink. In time each will ignite and add its light to the rest, and the cloud that made them will slowly be blown apart by their heat. The Lantern, in other words, is not a fixed thing. It is a process, caught part-way.

It is a lamp with its own flames inside.

Why your eye sees so little

The Lantern is large in the sky but its light is spread thin, and your eye judges a faint object by how bright each patch of it is, not by its total. A glow stretched over that much sky barely registers. Two more things are against you. Below a certain brightness the colour cells in your eye give up and the rod cells take over, and rods are sensitive but colour-blind, which is why every nebula looks grey to the naked eye, however colourful its pictures. And much of the Lantern's light is not visible at all: the warm dust shines in infrared, at wavelengths longer than red, which no eye can see.

A camera behind a telescope has none of those limits. It can gather light for hours, adding faint glow to faint glow, and it can be built to see in infrared. Brightwater's telescopes are built for exactly that, which is why their pictures look nothing like the view from the terrace.

Reading the false colours

Infrared has no colour of its own, so any picture made in it has to be given one. The convention at Brightwater is simple, and once you know it the pictures become maps rather than decorations.

Brightwater's colour key

  • Green: warm dust, heated by the stars nearby
  • Red: the hottest glowing gas, where young stars are fiercest
  • Blue: starlight, from stars in and behind the cloud
  • White: all three at once, usually a cluster at work
  • Black: cold, thick dust that hides whatever lies behind it

So the green cloud wrapped around a bright white core in the picture above is a shell of dust warmed by a cluster at its heart. The dark lanes cutting across it are not empty space but dust so cold and dense that nothing behind it shows through. None of these colours is what you would see if you could fly there. They are a translation, and a faithful one: every point in the picture is a measurement.

The regions, briefly

The Lantern's parts were named by observers long before Brightwater existed, and you will hear the names on any Lantern night. A quick introduction:

  • The Veil: the faint outer shell, a wide, thin curtain that shows only in long exposures.
  • The Witch: a long green profile along one flank, with a hooked nose if you are generous.
  • The Reef: a tangle of blue, orange and red, where glowing gas and warm dust overlap.
  • The Wing: a long green cloud with a bright red head, like a bird in a dive.
  • The Twin Fires: two bright clusters glowing white and green inside red dust.
  • The Nursery: where stars are still forming, dotted with bright knots.
  • The Butterfly: a red cloud of glowing gas with two spread lobes.

Where and when to see it

From Calder the Lantern is little more than a rumour. On the darkest nights, far from any town, a few keen observers claim to see it, but the air and the glow of the cities do the rest. Selka is airless and its sky is black even by day, yet Calder hangs in it, bright enough to cast shadows, and drowns the faint stuff.

Out at Tessaly the sky is darker. Ilyr is smaller and weaker, Veyra has no air at all, and Brightwater, on the moon's dark side, schedules its Lantern nights for when the nebula stands highest. After half an hour without a screen or a white lamp, most guests can see it unaided: a grey, faintly mottled glow with a brighter knot at one end. Binoculars show its shape. A telescope shows the Twin Fires as two separate points of light.

Two tips. Use red light only, because a single glance at a bright screen undoes twenty minutes of adapting. And look slightly to one side of the nebula rather than straight at it: the edge of your vision is more sensitive than its centre. Then, when you have seen the real thing, go indoors and look at the pictures. They will mean far more.

titles.en: Selka on foot: three days in the grey hills

descriptions.en: Two days from Halcyon, Calder's airless moon offers walkers a black sky at noon, the soft grey hills of the Taurin Valley and boot prints that will outlast them. Three days on foot from Camp Ardent.

bodies.en:
On Selka, the first thing you hear is your own breathing. The second is nothing at all. There is no wind on Calder's grey moon, no water and no birds, and when you stand still in the Taurin Valley at midday, under a sky as black as the inside of a pocket, the silence sits on your helmet like a hand. I walked there for three days from Camp Ardent, and I have been trying to describe it to people ever since.

Getting there, and Camp Ardent

The crossing from Halcyon Station takes two days, and ends at a landing field a short rover ride from camp. Camp Ardent is a pressurised hostel of 40 beds, half dug into a low hill: bunk rooms, a canteen with long tables, a suit room that smells of warm fabric and machine oil, and the guides' office, where a board lists every party outside and the time it is due back. Everyone who walks on Selka passes through it. Suits are rented here, guides hired here, and stories told here at night by people whose faces still carry the red line of a helmet seal.

Calder hangs in Selka's sky in the same place for the whole of your stay, blue and white and enormous, while Ilyr crawls so slowly across the black that over three days it barely moves. The camp keeps Port Kestrel time. Without it, you would lose track of the days within hours.

Day one: the suit, and the first steps

The fitting takes most of a morning. Technicians measure your shoulders, torso and hands, then bring the suit in pieces: legs, upper body, helmet, and the gloves, which matter more than anything else. A glove that is too long numbs your fingertips within an hour; one that is too short rubs the knuckles raw. Do not be polite about the fit. After a pressure check in a chamber comes the briefing: about eight hours of air per suit, the radio, the warning tones and what to do about each.

Then the airlock, and the first steps. Selka's gravity is about a sixth of Calder's, and your body has no idea what to do with it. You push off for a step and rise; you plant your foot and slide; you try to stop and keep going. Within half an hour most people find the guides' rolling lope, a sort of slow-motion skip, and start to enjoy themselves. In the afternoon we climbed the ridge behind the camp and looked down at our own tracks, sharp-edged in the grey dust. There is no wind here, and nothing to fill them: the prints you make on your first afternoon will still be there when your grandchildren come.

The prints you make on your first afternoon will still be there when your grandchildren come.

Day two: down into the Taurin Valley

The Taurin Valley is a broad trough of rolling grey hills, their outlines softened by ages of tiny impacts, a few hours' walk from camp. Our guide, a former survey technician named Pell Arandt, set an easy pace and stopped often. On Selka you need the stops. With no air to scatter the light, every shadow is pitch black, and a step into your own shadow can hide the ground completely. Distances are just as tricky. The horizon is close on so small a moon, and a hill that looks a short stroll away may take an hour to reach.

The colours are subtler than the pictures suggest. The dust is grey at noon, but in the low light near the valley floor it takes on a faint warm brown, and the old rover tracks from the survey years run across it in long double lines, as crisp as the day they were laid. Pell pointed out a set of boot prints by the trail and told us they were older than Camp Ardent. Nobody spoke for a while after that.

Lunch, such as it is, comes through a tube in your helmet: a sweet, thick drink that tastes better than it sounds after five hours of walking. By the time we were back at the airlock my thighs ached from all that bouncing, and I slept as well as I have anywhere.

Day three: the Sixth Station boulder

The last day's walk climbs a long grey slope to the Sixth Station boulder, named for the sixth of the old survey markers set beside it. It is the size of a house, split clean through the middle, and sits alone on the hillside under the black sky. A faint groove runs up the slope above it, the track it left when it rolled down from the ridge long before anyone came to see it. The gap between the two halves is wide enough for two people to stand in side by side. Guides let you step inside, one party at a time, and it is the quietest place I have ever been.

Back at camp, peeling off the suit, I noticed the smell it had brought in from outside, sharp and burnt, like spent matches. That is Selka's dust. It clings to everything and lingers in your nose for a day, and I found I did not mind at all.

Walking Selka

  • From Halcyon Station: 2 days
  • Camp Ardent: 40 beds, pressurised; book well ahead
  • Gravity: about a sixth of Calder's
  • Suits are rented at the camp; allow half a day for the fitting
  • Suit air: about 8 hours, so plan each day around it
  • Guides are hired at the camp; nobody walks beyond the ridge without one
  • Bring: thin liner gloves, soft socks, lip balm for the dry air indoors

titles.en: Why the crossing to Tessaly takes nine days, not three

descriptions.en: A liner could reach the ringed giant in three days if fuel were free. Our science correspondent explains transfer orbits, the 26-day launch windows and what the express really buys you.

bodies.en:
Every few weeks a letter reaches this magazine asking, more or less politely, why the crossing from Halcyon to Tessaly takes nine days when the liners have fusion drives and the giant, on a clear night, looks close enough to touch. The short answer is fuel. The longer answer is one of the most elegant ideas in travel, and it explains the timetable, the fares and the view from your cabin window.

The three-day crossing nobody flies

Suppose you point a liner at Tessaly and run the drive the whole way: accelerate for half the journey, turn round and brake for the other half. A modern ship could do it in about three days. The trouble is the bill. To halve the time of a journey you must roughly double your top speed, and then shed all of it again before you arrive. Worse, the propellant needed does not grow in step with the speed but much faster, because every tonne you burn early on has had to carry, and push, all the tonnes you have not burned yet.

Run the numbers and a three-day ship would need tanks larger than its cabins, and tickets priced like a small house. Nobody builds one. Instead, the liners borrow a trick from the worlds themselves.

Falling around Ilyr

Calder, Tessaly and everything else in the Reach are falling around Ilyr all the time, moving sideways fast enough that they never fall in. A liner leaving Halcyon is already doing the same, carried along at Calder's speed. It burns its drive hard for a few hours, which lifts it from Calder's path into a wider, oval one, and then the drive goes quiet and the ship coasts. It is still circling Ilyr, but on an orbit whose far end touches Tessaly's. Days later, at that point, it burns again to match the giant's speed and slips into orbit around it.

The coast costs nothing. That is the elegance of it: most of the crossing is free, paid for by the push at the start. It is also why the journey takes nine days rather than three. A ship that is coasting is not speeding up, and the curved path is longer than the straight line it replaces.

Most of the crossing is free, paid for by the push at the start.

The catch is timing. Tessaly has to be at the meeting point when the liner gets there, so a ship can leave only when Calder and Tessaly stand in the right arrangement. They come back into it every 26 days. Miss a window and you wait for the next one, which is why the departures gallery on Halcyon is crowded around each window and quiet in between.

Standard or express?

Both kinds of crossing fall around Ilyr. The difference is how hard they push.

Standard transfer

About nine days from Halcyon to Tessaly orbit.

  • Short burns at each end, a long free coast between
  • Cabins on spinning rings for almost the whole trip
  • The fare most travellers pay
  • Departures in every 26-day window

Express

About six days, on a steeper, faster path.

  • Longer burns, roughly three times the propellant
  • Fewer passengers and less cargo per sailing
  • Fares around two and a half times the standard
  • The same 26-day windows: speed does not free you from them

Most of the express's extra cost is paid at the far end. A ship that arrives fast must brake hard, and braking takes as much propellant as speeding up did, so the express carries fuel for both and has less room for anything else. That is the real price of the three days you save: not the drive, but everything the ship could have carried instead.

Is the express worth it? For a business trip, perhaps. For a holiday, the three days you save are three days of the best part of the journey: the coast, with nothing to do but read, eat and watch the giant grow.

What you see on the way

For the first day, Calder dominates the view astern, a blue-white disc shrinking hour by hour, with Halcyon a moving spark beside it and Selka a grey bead further off. Then the home world becomes a bright star, and Ilyr is the only large thing in the sky. It too grows a little smaller each day as you climb outward, and the light through the sunward windows turns noticeably paler.

By the fourth day Tessaly is the brightest point ahead, and with binoculars you can see that it is not quite round: the rings stretch it sideways. By the sixth it is a disc, banded and pale gold, and its moons show as points strung along the ring plane. On the last day it fills the window, the crew calls everyone to their seats for the braking burn, and for a few hours the floor seems to tilt as the drive adds its push to the ring's spin.

Time your crossing near Tessaly's equinox and the rings will be nearly edge-on when you arrive, a thin bright line drawn across the planet's face, as in the picture above. It is a reminder of how thin those rings are, and of how far you have come, for free, by falling.

titles.en: Inside the Long Window: Halcyon's observation deck after the refit

descriptions.en: Halcyon's 300-metre observation deck has reopened after its refit. What has changed, what you will see through the new glass, how to behave on the deck and how to book a dawn session.

bodies.en:
The first time Calder comes round beneath your feet, you will probably grab the rail. The Long Window, Halcyon Station's observation deck, is a curved sweep of glass 300 metres long set into the floor and outer wall of the Rim deck, and because the station turns once every 70 seconds, the whole sky wheels past it: stars, then the bright blue edge of the home world, then the planet itself, then stars again. After a long refit the deck has reopened, and it is better than ever.

What the refit changed

The old panes had served for longer than most of the station's staff have been alive, and it showed. Countless grains of dust, each far smaller than a grain of sand, had pitted the outer layers, and when Ilyr was close to the window a milky haze spread across the glass. Every pane has now been replaced with new laminated glass, thicker than before and clear enough that on the night side people instinctively step back from the edge.

The new glass also darkens itself in the instant Ilyr crosses it. Once every turn, for two or three seconds, the deck dims, as if the station had blinked, and then the view returns. It sounds like a gimmick. In practice it means you can stay by the window through the bright part of each turn without squinting, and it protects the eyes of anyone foolish enough to stare.

Inside, the café counter that used to fill one end of the deck has gone, moved to a bar outside the doors, and with it the clatter of cups. The lighting now falls to a low red glow during sessions, with guide strips along the floor. Along the glass are padded couches, and in the floor itself, sections where you are welcome to lie down and watch the sky turn beneath you.

Seventy seconds

Everything you see from the Long Window comes in turns. Within a minute you will know the rhythm: the stars slide across, Calder's limb rises as a brilliant blue band, the planet passes below, and the band sinks away again. It is hypnotic, and regulars say the trick is to stop chasing the view and let it come back to you.

The trick is to stop chasing the view and let it come back to you.

Across the turns, a slower story unfolds. On the night side, the cities of Calder glow in threads along the coasts, and in the aurora season the polar lights show as green curtains over the planet's dark edge. Watch for a while and you will see Selka rise, a grey crescent climbing a little higher above the blue band each time it comes round, as in the picture above. Below your feet, out of sight, liners leave the dock beneath the departures gallery; a few minutes later you will see one as a moving point of light, and then, when its drive lights, a short white flare that drifts across the glass and is gone.

How to behave

The deck has always had its customs. The refit has made them rules.

  • No flash, ever. It bounces off the glass and spoils everyone's eyes for minutes. Set your camera to manual, rest it on the glass and shoot between turns.
  • Screens down to their dimmest. The staff will ask once, then ask you to leave.
  • Quiet hours mean quiet. A blue light over each door marks them, and they cover every dawn session. Speak in a whisper or not at all.
  • Shoes off on the glass floor. Soft socks are provided at the door; heels and grit scratch even the new panes.
  • No food or drink on the deck. Take your coffee at the bar outside.

Children are welcome, and most of them fall silent faster than the adults. If you find the turning view makes you dizzy, sit on a couch and watch the far end of the window rather than the floor beneath you.

When to go, and how to book

Any time is a good time, but the dawn sessions are the ones people cross the station for. Halcyon passes through Calder's shadow on each orbit, and when it comes out, sunrise breaks along the planet's edge in a band of red and gold that brightens with every turn until the whole limb is lit. The deck's board, and every hotel desk on the Promenade, lists the times. Dusk, when the station slips back into shadow, is quieter and nearly as fine.

The Long Window

  • Where: the Rim deck, a few minutes' walk from the Promenade
  • Open all day; entry is free outside the dawn sessions
  • Dawn sessions: limited places, a small charge, booked at the desk outside the doors or through your hotel
  • Bookings open three days ahead and the best dawns go within hours
  • Arrive 15 minutes early; the doors close when the session begins
  • No flash, no food, socks on the glass

If you are only changing ships at Halcyon, try for one session anyway, even an ordinary one at midday. Lie on the glass, let a few turns go by, and watch the home world come round beneath you. It is the cheapest great view in the Reach.

titles.en: Orrin's Gediz Rim trail, step by step

descriptions.en: Four days and 38 km along the rim of the Gediz canyon, from Corran's dome past Bolívar Pass to the view of Mount Halvard. Suits, huts, air, water, packing and fitness, day by day.

bodies.en:
The Gediz canyon is so deep that on a still morning its far wall fades into a haze the colour of weak tea, and so long that you can walk its rim for four days and see only part of it. The trail from Corran is the classic walk on Orrin: 38 km, three nights in pressurised huts, one pass of wind-carved sand and one mountain view you will not forget. I have walked it twice. Here is how to do it well.

Before you go

Corran, the domed town on the canyon rim, is where every walker starts. Spend at least one full day there before setting out. You will need it for the suit fitting and the trail briefing, and your body will be glad of the time to settle after the crossing. Orrin's air is far too thin and cold to breathe, so outside the dome you wear a pressure suit at all times, and it is the suit, not the distance, that makes this walk hard work. It resists every bend of the knee and every closing of the hand. The gravity is lighter than Calder's, which helps, but the bulk more than makes up for it.

As for fitness: if you can walk 15 km with a day pack on two days running at home, you can do this. Practise in heavy gloves if you can, and work on your grip. Suits are hired in Corran with their air and water systems; you bring everything that goes inside them.

The trail has one rule, and the wardens enforce it: never leave a hut without a full air supply, and turn back if you reach a day's halfway marker with less than half. Each warden radios ahead when you set off, and the next hut knows when to expect you.

Day one: Corran to the Ochre hut, 9 km

You leave through Corran's main airlock after breakfast, and within ten minutes the dome is behind a fold of red-brown ground and you are alone with the rim. The first day is gentle on purpose. The path keeps a safe distance from the edge and crosses a wide valley scattered with dark rocks and low layered hills, the landscape most people picture when they think of Orrin. Every so often it swings out to a viewpoint, and the canyon opens below you: wall after wall of banded rock, falling away into shadow.

The Ochre hut, like all three on the trail, is a low pressurised shelter with an airlock, a rack for suits, sixteen bunks, a galley stocked with food and a warden who will check your seals before you sleep. Brush every grain of dust off your suit in the airlock before you go inside. Orrin's dust is fine as flour and gets into everything; the wardens are strict about it, and they are right.

Day two: through Bolívar Pass, 11 km

The longest day, and the most varied. After a few hours on the rim the trail drops to Bolívar Pass, where the wind has carved the sand into long, sharp-crested ridges that run in parallel below dark layered cliffs. Walking between them feels like moving through the ribs of something enormous. The sand is loose on the ridges' flanks, so stay on the marked line in the troughs and use your poles. In the afternoon wind the crests smoke with fine dust, which is beautiful and also a reason not to linger.

The Pass hut sits at the far end, where the trail climbs back towards the rim. Drink properly that evening. Inside a suit you sweat more than you notice, and the air in the huts is dry. The suit's drinking tube holds about three litres; empty it every day, and refill it every night.

Day three: the Halvard view, 10 km

Most walkers remember this day for a single moment. An hour beyond the Pass hut, the trail turns a shoulder of rock and Mount Halvard appears across the canyon: a layered mountain 5 km high, rising in reddish bands from the haze under a pale blue-grey sky. It does not look real at first. Your eye has nothing to measure it against, and only when you pick out a single band and follow it do you begin to see the size of the thing.

The path follows the rim for the rest of the day with the mountain in view almost all the way, and nobody hurries. The Halvard hut has a wide window facing the canyon. If the dust is right, stay up for the sunset, when the sky around the small, pale sun turns blue as the light fades.

Day four: to the rover halt, 8 km

The last morning is mostly downhill, away from the rim and across open ground to the rover halt at the trail's end, where a pressurised rover takes walkers back to Corran in about two hours. Most people are quiet on that ride. Your legs will ache, your hands most of all, and you will want a long wash in the dome. Book the bath before you leave town.

What to pack

  • Two sets of thin base layers: one to walk in, one for the huts
  • Liner gloves and a spare pair; they take the wear, not your skin
  • Soft, well-worn walking socks, three pairs
  • Blister plasters, tape and something for sore hands
  • Hut slippers and a light sleeping-bag liner
  • Snacks that can be eaten through the suit's feeding port
  • A small brush for dust, and patience for using it
  • The pack rides over the suit, so keep it light: 8 kg is plenty

titles.en: The Rose: chasing the storm at Tessaly's pole

descriptions.en: At Tessaly's north pole, a storm called the Rose turns inside a six-sided jet stream. What it is, why the frame has six sides, why its pictures are false colour and how liners line up the view.

bodies.en:
Of all the sights in the Reach, the Rose is the one most often called impossible. A storm thousands of kilometres across turns at the top of Tessaly, and around it, like a frame around a painting, runs a jet stream with six straight sides. Nature does not do straight lines, people say. Here it does, and it has been doing so for as long as anyone has looked. As a geologist I was trained to distrust anything that looks too tidy. The Rose is tidy, and it is real.

A storm at the top of the world

The Rose is a polar vortex: a vast, long-lived storm sitting exactly on Tessaly's north pole. Its eye is about 2,000 km across, and its spiral arms reach far beyond that, winding inward towards a centre where the clouds dip deep into the planet. At the eye wall the winds run at several hundred kilometres an hour.

Storms on Calder are born over warm water and die when they reach land or cool sea. The Rose has neither to stop it. Tessaly has no surface, only deeper and denser layers of gas, and nothing beneath the storm to drag on it. The planet spins fast, once every 10.5 hours or so, and that spin, together with the heat rising from deep inside the giant, keeps the storm fed. Nobody knows how old the Rose is. Every record of Tessaly's pole shows it there.

Why six sides

Further from the pole, a narrow river of wind races around the planet: a jet stream. On most worlds a jet like this wanders in loose, shifting loops. Tessaly's settles into a hexagon, each side about 14,000 km long, and holds it.

The reason lies in the difference in speed. The jet is a fast stream with slower air on either side, and wherever fast fluid runs beside slow, waves form along the boundary, as they do where a quick river meets still water. Under the right conditions, set by the jet's speed, its width and the planet's spin, those waves lock into a pattern that stays fixed in place, with a fixed number of crests. Tessaly's numbers give six.

Nature does not do straight lines, people say. Here it does.

You can watch the same thing happen in a laboratory. Fill a shallow tank with water on a turntable, spin a ring at its centre a little faster than the rest, add dye, and polygons appear in the swirl: three sides, four, five, six, more, depending on the speeds. Students at Port Kestrel do it in a morning. It never stops being strange.

The hexagon also keeps time. It turns with the deep interior of the planet, steadily, while the clouds elsewhere drift with the winds, and its turning is one of the ways astronomers worked out the length of a Tessaly day.

Why the pictures are not what you will see

The famous image of the Rose, a deep-red spiral in a sea of green cloud, is false colour. It is made in infrared, through filters tuned to wavelengths that the gases of Tessaly's atmosphere partly absorb. Light reflected from deep clouds has to pass through more gas on its way out, so it arrives dimmer in those bands than light from high clouds. Each colour in the picture, in other words, stands for a height. In the usual convention red marks the deep cloud seen down the throat of the storm, and green the high haze all around it.

Such pictures are maps of the storm's shape in three dimensions, which is why scientists love them. They are not a promise of what the window will show.

To the eye, from a liner, the Rose is subtler: soft gold and cream with grey-blue shadows, the eye a darker well at the centre, the spiral clear in binoculars. The hexagon shows as a faint change of tone along its edges, easiest to see when Ilyr is low over the pole and the cloud tops cast long shadows.

Lining up the view

Most liners arrive at Tessaly in the plane of its rings, heading for Veyra and the other moons, and from there the pole is seen at a steep slant, if at all. Sailings that offer the Rose make a polar pass. They shape the braking burn so that the arrival orbit swings high over the north, at the cost of a few extra hours and a little extra propellant, which is why the pass usually carries a surcharge. The best of the view lasts a few hours around the high point of that orbit, with the pole almost directly below.

Season matters too. The Rose must be in sunlight to be seen at all, and during the long northern winter it sits in darkness. Near equinox, when the rings go edge-on, Ilyr skims the horizon at the pole, the light is low and the shadows long, and the hexagon is at its clearest. A pass that also carries the liner through Tessaly's shadow brings a second reward: the giant backlit by Ilyr, its rings glowing like a halo.

Seeing the Rose

  • Where: Tessaly's north pole, inside the six-sided jet stream
  • Size: the eye about 2,000 km across; each side of the hexagon about 14,000 km
  • Best from: a liner's polar pass, a few hours around the high point
  • When: whenever the pole is sunlit; the low light near equinox shows the hexagon best
  • Bring: binoculars, and patience; the details come slowly

titles.en: Veyra: walking among the ice geysers

descriptions.en: At Veyra's south pole, ice sprays into space from long fractures called the Tiger Lines. A guided walk across the geyser field, the rhythm of the plumes and why you want to see them backlit.

bodies.en:
The first plume I saw on Veyra rose without a sound. It came from a seam in the ice some way ahead of us, a pale column that thickened, leaned and kept on rising long after my eyes said it should have fallen back. On a moon with almost no gravity, ice does not so much fall as drift, and the jets from Veyra's south pole climb hundreds of kilometres before they thin into the black. We had been walking for an hour. Our guide stopped, turned and simply pointed.

The Tiger Lines

Veyra is a small, bright moon of Tessaly, wrapped in clean ice that throws back nearly all the light that falls on it. At its south pole a set of long, parallel fractures cuts across the surface: the Tiger Lines, each well over a hundred kilometres long. They are less cold than the ice around them, because beneath Veyra's shell lies liquid water, kept from freezing by the constant flexing of the moon as it circles the giant. Water vapour and grains of ice escape through the fractures and spray out into space, and some of it falls back as snow so fine that it settles like flour.

From the ground the Lines are less dramatic than their name. They show as low ridges, a few dark seams and a softening of the ice on either side where the fallen snow lies deepest. It is only when a plume rises that you understand you are standing on a lid.

Walking the field

Walks start from the polar shelter, a pressurised hut and landing pad at the edge of the geyser field. They are guided, always, in groups of up to eight, and they never go close to the fractures themselves: the ground near the Lines is soft and the edges unstable, and the guides keep their parties well back, on ice they have walked for years. You do not need to be close. The plumes are so tall that they fill the sky from a distance.

Moving is the first lesson. Veyra's gravity is so slight that a careless step can launch you several metres and leave you drifting down for what feels like an age, so each walker is clipped to a line, and boots have weighted soles and short spikes. The rhythm is a slow, deliberate shuffle. It is tiring in a way that walking at home never is, and most people are glad of the break in the shelter at the halfway point.

The cold is the second lesson. The surface is around minus 200 degrees, and although the suits are heated, the cold finds the places where they touch you: the fingertips, the toes, the back of the neck against the helmet ring. Wear the liner gloves you are given and tell the guide early if your hands start to go numb. They have seen every kind of brave silence, and they would rather you spoke.

The rhythm of the plumes

The geysers are not steady. Veyra's orbit around Tessaly is slightly oval, and the tides that squeeze the moon change as it goes round. At the far point of each orbit the fractures are pulled open a little wider and the plumes swell; near the close point they narrow and the jets dim. The whole cycle repeats every orbit, about a day and a half, and the guides time the walks so that you are out on the field as the plumes build.

Within that rhythm, single jets come and go on their own. One may fall silent for hours and then return, stronger, in a slightly different place. Part of the pleasure of a second walk is learning to read the field as the guides do, noticing which vents are awake.

It is only when a plume rises that you understand you are standing on a lid.

Seeing them backlit

Here is the secret of every great picture of Veyra's plumes, including the one above: the light comes from behind them. Grains of ice scatter light forward, as dust does in a sunbeam, so the plumes look faint with Ilyr at your back and brilliant with Ilyr behind them. On the ground, the best moment comes when Ilyr has just dropped below the horizon. The sky goes black, the surface goes dark, and the jets light up in tall, glowing columns against the night. Guides will position the group for it, and they will ask for complete silence on the radio while it lasts.

The approach by shuttle is often timed for the same effect, with the plumes seen edge-on against black space as the craft comes in. Ask for a window seat on the side away from Ilyr.

Staying at Brightwater

Most walkers stay at Brightwater, the observatory and small lodge on Veyra's dark side, and fly to the polar shelter for the day by surface shuttle, a short hop in so little gravity. The lodge has only a handful of rooms and fills well ahead, so book it first and build the rest of the trip around it. On the nights between walks there are the Lantern nights, when the observatory opens its telescopes to guests and the great nebula hangs over the ice. After a day among the geysers, it is a gentle way to end.

Walking the geyser field

  • Getting there: Tessaly is 9 days from Halcyon on the standard transfer
  • Base: Brightwater, on Veyra's dark side; a short shuttle hop to the pole
  • Walks: guided only, up to eight people, roped and spiked
  • Timing: plumes swell towards the far point of Veyra's orbit, about every day and a half
  • Best light: just after Ilyr sets, with the plumes backlit
  • Temperature: around minus 200 degrees; bring liner gloves and warm socks

titles.en: Blue hour on Orrin: why the sunsets turn blue

descriptions.en: Orrin's noon sky is butterscotch and its sunsets cold blue. Our science correspondent explains the dust behind it, where to watch near Corran and how to photograph it through a visor.

bodies.en:
On Orrin the colours of the sky run backwards. Noon is the shade of butterscotch, the horizon a dusty tan, and then, in the last minutes of the day, a cold blue glow gathers around the setting sun like frost on a window. Here is why it happens, and where to stand near Corran when it does.

A sky coloured by dust

On Calder we are used to a blue sky by day and a red one at sunset. Both are the air's doing. The gas scatters short, blue wavelengths far more strongly than long, red ones, so blue light is bounced around the whole dome of the sky, while a low sun, shining through a long slab of atmosphere, loses its blue on the way and turns orange.

Orrin's air is far too thin for that. Travellers wear pressure suits outside for good reason: there is barely enough gas there to scatter anything. What colours Orrin's sky is dust. The wind lifts very fine grains from the plains and canyon floors, most of them smaller than a thousandth of a millimetre, and keeps them aloft for weeks. As a geologist I find them lovely things: flakes of weathered rock stained with iron, the same rust that makes the ground red. They also behave nothing like gas. They absorb a good share of the blue light that reaches them, and they scatter what is left mostly forward, in the direction it was already travelling, rather than out across the sky.

Butterscotch at noon, blue at dusk

At midday the sun is high and its light takes a short path through the dust. The grains soak up blue and spread the warmer colours widely, so the whole sky takes on the pale caramel tone that visitors find either cosy or faintly unsettling. Shadows are sharp, and the ground, already red-brown, looks redder still.

As the sun drops, its light crosses far more dust before it reaches you, and the forward scattering takes over. Blue light, which these grains throw into a tight cone around the direction of the sun, arrives as a glow gathered close around the disc. Away from the sun the sky fades to grey-brown. The effect is strongest in the half hour either side of sunset, and it is not subtle. The small, pale sun sinks inside a halo of blue that can spread to several times its width.

A useful way to remember it: on Calder the blue is everywhere except near the setting sun; on Orrin it is nowhere except near the setting sun. The blue is not the air. It is the dust, and the dust changes from week to week.

That last point matters when you plan. Straight after a dust storm the sky is loaded and the blue is wide, soft and rather washed out. After a long calm, when much of the dust has settled, the glow tightens and deepens. Corran's weather office chalks a daily dust reading on the board beside the main lock; a middling figure, a few days after a storm, tends to give the finest evenings.

Where to watch near Corran

Corran sits on the rim of the Gediz canyon, and near the town the canyon runs roughly east to west. That is a gift to anyone who likes a sunset: on most evenings the sun goes down along it, over the far rim, with the whole depth of the canyon in front of you.

  • The west gallery of the dome. No suit, no booking: a bench, a hot drink and a wall of glass. The glass softens the colours a little, but this is the easy first look, and on a clear evening the benches fill an hour before sunset.
  • The Weather Steps. A cut ledge twenty minutes' walk from the west lock, past the instrument masts, on a marked path with the canyon dropping away to your left. Suits are required, and so is a companion. This is where the town's photographers go.
  • The first trail hut. Walkers on the Gediz Rim trail spend their first night in a pressurised hut that looks straight down the canyon. If you are doing the four-day walk, you get blue hour without leaving the route.
  • Bolívar Pass. Further along the trail, the wind-carved sand ridges below the dark layered cliffs catch the last light in long stripes, and the blue glow sits just above them. It is for trail walkers only; there is no quick way out and back.
The small, pale sun sinks inside a halo of blue that can spread to several times its width.

Photographing the blue

Cameras record Orrin's sunsets more honestly than eyes do. Eyes adjust to the colour within minutes and start to see it as ordinary; a sensor never does. It does need some help, though.

  • Fix the white balance. Set it to daylight and leave it there. Automatic white balance decides the blue is a mistake and corrects it towards grey, and turns the butterscotch noon sky an unconvincing white.
  • Expose for the glow. Take your reading from the bright blue around the sun and let the ridge go black. Most cameras will try to brighten the foreground; give them a stop or two less than they ask for, and take a second frame darker still.
  • Mind the visor. A suit's outer sun visor is tinted gold, which turns blue into a muddy green. Raise the sun visor, never the pressure visor beneath it, and rest the lens hood gently against the clear inner visor so that the inside of your helmet does not reflect into the frame. Switch your helmet lamp off first.
  • Keep the batteries warm. The cold drains them fast. Carry a spare in an inner pocket of the suit's thermal layer and swap it once you are back inside the lock.
  • Use something steady. Gloved hands shake. A small tripod, or the low wall at the Weather Steps, makes a sharp picture far more likely as the light falls.

The blue lingers for twenty minutes or so after the sun has gone, shrinking to a band along the horizon, and some of the best pictures come in those last minutes. Agree a turn-back time with your group before you leave the lock, and keep to it: the path is marked, but it is easier to follow in the light.

Blue hour at a glance

  • Best time: the half hour either side of sunset
  • Best conditions: a middling dust reading, a few days after a storm
  • Easiest view: Corran's west gallery, no suit needed
  • Best view: the Weather Steps, 20 minutes from the west lock, suited and in pairs
  • Camera: daylight white balance, expose for the glow, gold visor raised
  • Bring: a spare battery in an inner pocket, a small tripod

titles.en: The aurora season on Calder, from above and below

descriptions.en: Green curtains, red fringes and seven weeks late in Calder's year: how to watch the aurora from a night flight out of Port Kestrel, or looking down from Halcyon's Long Window.

bodies.en:
Late in Calder's year the sky over both poles starts to move. Curtains of green light ripple and fold, their upper edges fringed with red, and for a few weeks the aurora is the finest show on the home world. There are two ways to watch it: from a darkened aircraft flying beneath it, or from Halcyon Station, looking down. I have done both many times, and I still cannot choose.

What lights the sky

Ilyr does not only shine. It also breathes out a constant, thin stream of charged particles, steady on most days and gusty on others, when the star throws off a burst. Calder's magnetic field turns most of that stream aside, but near the poles the field lines dip down into the atmosphere, and there the particles follow them in. They strike the upper air between about 100 and 300 km up, and the air glows.

The colours tell you the height. Oxygen in the lower part of that band gives the familiar green, the colour of almost every aurora picture you have seen. Higher up, where the air is thinnest, oxygen glows red instead, which is why the tops of the curtains are fringed with crimson. On strong nights nitrogen adds a pink-violet hem along the bottom edge, and the whole curtain seems to ripple as the incoming stream changes.

The particles arrive in a ring around each pole, not at the pole itself. Seen from below, that ring is an arc across the sky. Seen from above, it is a crown of light lying on the night side of the planet.

Why late in the year

The aurora never entirely stops, but it is not spread evenly through the year. Late in Calder's year, around the turn of the seasons, the planet's magnetic field sits at an angle to Ilyr's stream that lets far more of it in, and the displays at both poles grow brighter and more frequent at the same time. The season lasts about seven weeks. Within it, activity still rises and falls from night to night, depending on what Ilyr is doing, and no forecast more than three days ahead is better than a good guess.

From above you are reading it like a map.

So build in some slack. If you are booking a single flight, book it in the middle weeks of the season. If you are watching from Halcyon, stay at least three nights.

Two ways to see it

From below

Aurora flights leave Port Kestrel in the evening throughout the season. The Kestrel sits on the equator, so the first part of the night is a long run towards the pole; then the aircraft spends about two hours beneath the arc, turning slowly so that both sides of the cabin get their share, before the long flight home. Expect around twelve hours in all.

From below you are inside the display. The curtains hang overhead and ahead, they move faster than you expect, and on a strong night the light is bright enough to read by. The cabin lights go off as you reach the arc. Window seats on the poleward side cost more and are worth it.

From above

From Halcyon's Long Window the aurora is a band of green on Calder's night side, lying close along the curve of the limb, with its red upper layer seen edge-on as a thin glowing line above the planet. On a good night you can follow the arc for thousands of kilometres.

From above you are reading it like a map. The changes are slower and stranger: brightenings that run along the arc like a lit fuse, patches that pulse on and off. There is no flight and no weather, and you can come back every night of your stay.

What to wear and bring

On the flights, cabins are kept cool after dark so the inner window panes stay clear of mist, and you will be sitting still for hours, so bring a warm layer. Wear dark clothes: a pale sleeve reflects in the window and puts a ghost in every picture. Dim your screen to its lowest, or better, put it away; the crew will ask you to in any case.

The Long Window has its own rules: no flash, quiet hours, and the lights kept low along the gallery. Dark clothing helps there too, for the same reason. You will not need binoculars in either place. The aurora is big, and it is best seen whole. A small notebook is more use: people who write down what they saw at the time remember a great deal more of it.

Photographing the aurora

  • Focus by hand. Autofocus hunts in the dark. Set the lens to infinity, check it on a bright star, and tape the ring if you can.
  • Open up. Use your lens's widest aperture and a high sensitivity, and accept a little grain in exchange for sharpness.
  • Keep exposures short. An aircraft vibrates and a station turns. One or two seconds is plenty for a bright display; anything longer blurs the curtains into a green fog.
  • Get close to the glass. A soft rubber hood pressed against the window cuts out reflections. Without one, a dark scarf draped over lens and window does the same job.
  • Shoot hard, then stop. Take your pictures in the first bright burst, then put the camera down and watch. The best displays rarely last longer than a quarter of an hour, and you will want to have seen them.

Aurora season essentials

  • When: late in Calder's year, for about seven weeks
  • From below: evening aurora flights from Port Kestrel, about 12 hours in all, two of them under the arc
  • From above: Halcyon's Long Window; stay three nights or more
  • Colours: green from oxygen low down, red fringes higher up, a pink hem on strong nights
  • Wear: warm, dark layers, nothing pale on your sleeves
  • Camera: manual focus at infinity, widest aperture, exposures of one or two seconds

titles.en: A week aboard the Morning Lark, the slowest liner in the Reach

descriptions.en: Fourteen days to Tessaly, bread before the first watch, three thousand books and a captain who calls speed a fuel bill: the second week aboard the Reach's slowest liner.

bodies.en:
The Morning Lark takes fourteen days to reach Tessaly. The quicker liners do it in nine, and not one of her 120 passengers seemed to mind. I sailed with her from Halcyon for the whole crossing, but it is the second week I want to tell you about: the week when the ship stopped being a novelty and turned into a small, well-fed town.

A slow ship, on purpose

I spent nine years inspecting hulls at the Halcyon yards, and I tend to judge a ship by her seams before her saloons. The Lark's seams are old and very good. She is not fast and was never meant to be. Where the standard transfer to Tessaly takes nine days, she flies a long, gentle loop that stretches the voyage to fourteen, and her owners decided long ago to make the extra days the point rather than the price.

By day eight the routines have set. The ship's bell sounds the watches. The lights along the ring dim at ship's evening and brighten slowly before breakfast, so that by the second week nobody needs an alarm. Every cabin is on the spinning ring, and the outer ring, where the weight is nearly full, is where most people sleep best; the few cabins nearest the drive section are cheaper, and you can hear why.

The galley keeps the clock

If the bell is the Lark's clock, the galley is her heart. Bread comes out of the ovens before the first watch, and the smell reaches the far end of the ring before the lights come up. Breakfast and lunch are served at long shared tables. Dinner is two sittings, and you keep the same table for the voyage, which is how friendships start.

On a fast liner you are in transit. On the Lark you are somewhere.

The head cook, Arno Pell, has been aboard longer than most of the crew, and he plans his menus around the voyage itself. The first week runs on fresh produce loaded from Halcyon's hydroponic gardens. By day ten the salads give way to roasted roots, slow stews and the galley's own pickles, and the herbs that grow under lamps beside the galley windows go into everything. On the twelfth evening there is a long dinner that the crew call the loop supper, eaten as the ship begins her final curve towards Tessaly. I will not spoil the menu, except to say that there is a pudding, and that people talk about it on Halcyon.

The library, and the people in it

The Lark's other famous room is her library: a little over three thousand printed books, a wall of star charts, and deep armchairs bolted to the deck in case the spin is ever trimmed. Its windows look out on the shadow side, so the light is always soft. In the mornings it is silent. After lunch it becomes the ship's sitting room, with a chess ladder pinned to the door and an unofficial waiting list for the armchair nearest the window.

That is where I came to know my fellow passengers. A retired surveyor, travelling to see rings she had once helped to map from a desk on Calder. A young astronomer bound for Brightwater on Veyra, who gave an impromptu talk about the Lantern that ran an hour over and that nobody wanted to end. A couple from Calder's northern coast who had saved for six years for the trip, planned every day of it, and abandoned the plan by day four. Two children who learned cards from one of the ship's engineers and then beat him, repeatedly. On a fast liner you are in transit. On the Lark you are somewhere.

Captain Okoro's ship

Captain Ines Okoro walks the full ring every morning, alone and at a brisk pace, and on most evenings she takes questions in the library for half an hour. She is patient with the first-timers and more patient still with those of us who ask about pump pressures. When I asked her why the Lark had never been refitted for speed, she looked at me as if I had suggested painting over a window. "Fast is a fuel bill," she said. "Slow is a timetable. People can live inside a timetable."

On day eleven she took a small group of us through the drive section, ear defenders on, and I was quietly pleased to find the shielding plates freshly inspected and stamped by my old yard. It is not a glamorous thing to notice, but it is the reason a ship of her age still sails.

Day fourteen: into the shadow of the rings

Tessaly had been a bright star, then a disc, then a world. On the last morning the galley served breakfast at the windows, which I had never seen done on any ship. The Lark's loop brings her in high, so the rings lie below you, sweeping all the way round the planet, and across them falls the long, sharp shadow of Tessaly itself, a dark band cut cleanly through the ice. You can watch the cloud bands turn as you close in; a day there lasts only about ten and a half hours, and over the course of breakfast a pale storm on the limb crept visibly towards us.

Nobody spoke much. Then the bell rang for the approach watch, the spell broke, and people began to swap addresses across their tables. I have crossed to Tessaly many times, and never so slowly, and never so well fed.

titles.en: Port Kestrel on a budget

descriptions.en: Dorm beds from 30 marks, noodles for 6 and the best launch view in the Reach for nothing: a former hostel keeper's guide to doing Port Kestrel cheaply.

bodies.en:
Port Kestrel is where most journeys in the Reach begin, and it is perfectly possible to spend more on two nights there than on a week almost anywhere else. It is just as possible not to. I used to run a hostel beside the launch pads, and these are the things my guests learned, usually the expensive way, until I started telling them on arrival.

Where to sleep: the Old Docks

Forget the towers along the shuttle halls. The bargains are in the Old Docks quarter, a grid of former cargo warehouses a short walk from the pads, where most buildings now hold hostels on the upper floors and something to eat at street level. A bed in a shared dorm costs 30 to 45 marks a night; a private capsule with a fan, a lock and a shelf for your bag runs from 70 to 90. Book direct: the hostels pay a cut to the booking boards, and many will knock a few marks off if you simply message them or turn up.

Ask three things before you pay. Is there a fan or cooling? The Kestrel is on the equator, and the old warehouses hold the day's heat well into the night. Which side faces the pads? Launches are loud, and a pad-side room means a rattle in the window at odd hours, which some people love and some very much do not. And will they keep your bag on the day you fly? Most Old Docks hostels store luggage free until your shuttle, which saves you the fee at the halls.

Where to eat: night markets and noodle counters

Port Kestrel eats late, after the heat breaks. The night markets set up in the old loading yards at dusk and run until the small hours: grilled skewers, flatbreads off a hot plate, cut fruit from the coast, sweet fried dough in paper cones. Most plates cost 4 to 10 marks, and the stalls with the longest queues are the right ones.

By day, look for the noodle counters along the dock road, where the pad crews eat at shift change. A bowl of broth noodles costs 6 to 9 marks and will carry you to evening; a pot of tea at the counter is 2. The crews know which counters are good and which are merely close to the halls, and they eat at the good ones.

The single best saving in the Kestrel is water. Every public square in the Old Docks has a free refill tap, and the shuttle halls have them past security. Bring a bottle and you will never again pay 4 marks for a small one.

The Upper Terraces: the best free show in the Reach

The Upper Terraces are public viewing decks stepped up the side of the pad complex, free and open day and night. From the top tier you look straight down onto the pads, and when a shuttle goes you see the light first, then feel the sound arrive a few seconds later through the soles of your feet. I have watched hundreds of launches from up there, and I still go whenever I am back.

Timing is everything. The launch boards in the Old Docks and at the foot of the Terraces list the day's departures. Evening and night launches are the most spectacular and the most crowded, so arrive 45 minutes early for a place at the rail. Midday launches are quieter, but the equatorial sun on the upper tiers is fierce and there is little shade, so bring a hat. And remember that a launch time is a hope, not a promise. Holds happen. Bring something to sit on and someone to talk to.

Getting to the shuttle halls

From the Old Docks, the halls are a twenty-minute walk along the dock road, or four stops on the dock tram, which costs 2 marks a ride. Leave earlier than you think you need to: check-in closes well before boarding, and the queue for baggage weighing on a busy morning is long. The limits are strict and enforced to the gram, so weigh your bag at the hostel (most have scales by the door) and wear your heaviest shoes rather than packing them.

Food inside the halls costs about three times what it does outside, so eat before you go. Keep it light: plain bread and tea a couple of hours before boarding is what I told every guest, and nobody ever came back to complain.

More ways to keep the marks in your pocket

  • Arrive the day before. A missed shuttle costs far more than a night in a dorm.
  • Eat your main meal at noon. Many noodle counters do a set lunch, a bowl and a side, for less than the evening price.
  • Skip the observation bars. The bars in the hall towers charge for the same view the Terraces give away.
  • Walk at night. The Old Docks are busy and cooler after dark, and the tram stops running long before the markets close.
  • Pack light for the climb. Every extra kilo is something you will carry six hours up to Halcyon and, eventually, back down again.

Port Kestrel prices, in marks

  • Dorm bed in the Old Docks: 30–45 a night
  • Private capsule: 70–90 a night
  • Night-market plate: 4–10
  • Bowl of broth noodles: 6–9
  • Pot of tea at a counter: 2
  • Dock tram ride: 2
  • Left luggage at the shuttle halls: 15 a day (often free at your hostel)
  • Upper Terraces: free, always

And when, a few minutes after launch, the night side of Calder curves away beneath your window under the pale band of the galaxy, you will find that the best view of the whole trip costs nothing extra at all.

titles.en: Thule, the orange moon nobody visits (yet)

descriptions.en: Tessaly's orange moon hides its stars and the giant overhead. Fewer than thirty people a year go down to Amber Camp: here is what they do there, and how to join them.

bodies.en:
Most travellers to Tessaly see Thule exactly once: a small orange coin sliding across the giant's pale bands, glimpsed from a lounge window on the way to Veyra. Fewer than thirty people a year go further, under permit, down through the haze to Amber Camp. I was one of six this season, and I suspect that in a few years the number will be a great deal larger.

A moon wrapped in fog

From orbit Thule has no features at all. It is a smooth ball of orange haze, a little darker towards the poles, with nothing beneath it showing. The haze is a kind of high smog, made when Ilyr's light breaks apart the gases at the top of Thule's thick atmosphere and the fragments recombine into fine, sticky particles. They drift down for years and gather in layers, and the result is a sky that hides everything.

Underneath it, the light is the first surprise. Noon on Thule is a dim, even amber, like the last half hour of an autumn afternoon on Calder, and it barely changes from one hour to the next. There are no shadows to speak of. There are no stars. And somewhere overhead, filling a great slice of the sky, hangs Tessaly, rings and all, which you will not see once from the surface. You are standing beneath a ringed giant, and you cannot see it. Some visitors find that maddening. Most, by the second day, find it oddly restful.

The cold, and Amber Camp

The second surprise is the cold, which is beyond anything on Calder: well below minus 170 degrees at the surface, day and night. The air is thick, much thicker than Calder's, so suits here are about heat and breathing rather than pressure. They are heavier and warmer than the suits you may know from Selka or Orrin, with heated gloves and boots, and an hour outside feels like a full day's work.

You are standing beneath a ringed giant, and you cannot see it.

Amber Camp is a research station first and a guest house a distant second. Its modules sit on a low rise above a frost plain, joined by insulated tunnels, and most of its people are there to study the haze: how it forms, how it falls, how it changes over Thule's long seasons. Visitors sleep in a single guest module of six bunks, eat in the shared mess with the researchers and take their turn at the washing-up. It is warm, cramped, sociable and a little chaotic, and nobody I met there wanted it any other way.

What visitors actually do

There are no sights in the usual sense, and the camp is honest about that. What there is, is the work, and guests are invited to share it.

  • Balloon launches. Most mornings the camp sends a small instrument balloon up into the haze. Guests help to fill and release it, and in the thick, cold air it rises with an odd, unhurried grace.
  • Walks on the frost plain. With a researcher, never alone, out along a line of marker poles. The ground crunches underfoot, and the haze swallows the camp behind you within a few hundred metres.
  • Sampling. Collecting the fine orange dust that settles on trays set out around the camp. It is the haze itself, fallen.
  • Listening. Sound carries well in thick air, and the plain is so quiet that you can hear the camp's fans from a long way off, and your own breathing above everything.

And every so often the haze thins. It happened once during our ten days, for about an hour: the amber lifted a shade, and a faint, banded paleness appeared high in the sky, where Tessaly was. Two of the researchers, who had been there for months, put down their work and came out to watch it with us.

Amber Camp asks every visitor to accept that the research comes first. Balloon launches move with the weather, walks are cancelled if a researcher is needed elsewhere, and the guest module is the first thing given up if the camp runs short of space.

How to get a permit

Permits are issued by the camp's research council, for stays of about ten days, six visitors at a time and only a few times a year. The application asks for a medical certificate, some evidence of suit experience (a walk on Selka or Orrin counts) and a short note on why you want to go. The council reads every one. Getting there means the standard nine-day transfer from Halcyon to Tessaly, and then a seat on one of the camp's supply landers, which run to the camp's schedule rather than yours: allow several days either side.

It is not cheap, it is not comfortable, and there is no lodge with a view at the end of it. That is precisely why it is worth going now.

The next Veyra?

It is worth remembering that Veyra, not so long ago, was much like this: an observatory with a few bunks and a handful of guests a year. Brightwater is still small, but its Lantern nights are now famous, and Veyra's Glass Shore has only just opened to small guided groups. Thule could follow the same path. The camp's researchers half expect it, and are divided about it. Some would welcome the visitors and the funding they bring. Others, quite reasonably, would like the plain to stay as quiet as it is now.

For the moment, Thule remains the moon that almost everyone has seen and almost nobody has visited. Go while that is still true.

Thule in brief

  • What: Tessaly's orange moon, wrapped in a thick haze
  • Base: Amber Camp, a research camp with one guest module of six bunks
  • Permits: from the camp's research council; stays of about ten days, six visitors at a time, a few times a year
  • Getting there: 9 days from Halcyon to Tessaly on the standard transfer, then a camp supply lander
  • Conditions: thick, unbreathable air, well below minus 170 degrees; heated suits with their own air
  • Bring: proof of suit experience, patience, and a good book for weather days

titles.en: Mirren: forty days to the edge of the Reach

descriptions.en: One sailing a year, forty days out and twelve guest berths at Hollin Station: aboard the Long Swan to Mirren's ice mountains, nitrogen plains and stacked blue haze.

bodies.en:
Once a year the expedition ship Long Swan leaves Tessaly for Mirren, the frozen world at the outer edge of the Reach. The passage takes about forty days, the stay at Hollin Station a little under three weeks, and the whole voyage, from Tessaly and back, the best part of a hundred days. I had spent nine years looking at ships in dock. I wanted, once, to see what a hull goes through on the longest regular voyage in the Reach.

The long passage

Most of us joined the Swan in orbit at Tessaly, after the usual nine days from Halcyon, and for the first few days the giant and its rings still filled the aft windows. Then they shrank. By the second week Tessaly was a bright, slightly oval star, and Ilyr itself was noticeably smaller and whiter than it looks from Calder. By the fourth week the Lantern, which hangs faintly in the night sky of the outer Reach, had become the most interesting thing in the forward window, and the ship's small telescope was booked from ship's evening until the small hours.

Forty days with nothing outside sounds like a hardship, and the crew are frank that it can be. The Swan's answer is routine. Everyone exercises for an hour a day, no exceptions, because the ship's spin ring is small, the weight it gives is light, and the body needs persuading to stay strong. There are talks most evenings, given by the Hollin researchers travelling out to their posts. There is a workshop where passengers learn to service suit joints and seals, which turned out to be the most popular class aboard, and which proved its worth later.

Life aboard the Long Swan

The Swan is small and built for the job rather than for show. She carries twelve guests, one for each of the guest berths waiting at Hollin Station, along with her crew and whichever researchers are rotating out that year. Cabins are compact; the mess is the centre of the ship; a single observation blister forward seats eight at a squeeze. Water is recycled with a thoroughness you stop noticing after a week. Food is good and plain and, by the last fortnight, largely grown or rehydrated aboard.

The chief engineer let me walk the hull inspections with her, which is not something she offers every guest, and I learned a good deal about how a ship is kept on a voyage this long. Long passages are hard on seals and bearings rather than on plating, and the Swan's crew check every pump and gasket on a rota that runs the full forty days. On day thirty-eight the drive came up for the long burn into Mirren's orbit, and the whole ship hummed for hours. At dinner that evening, for the first time, people talked about the arrival rather than the journey.

Hollin Station

Hollin Station sits on a shelf at the foot of the Hollin Range: a cluster of insulated modules half buried for warmth, a landing pad, a garage of rovers and a long, low common room facing the mountains. It is a research outpost first. Its twelve guest berths are filled once a year, by the Swan's passengers, and for the rest of the year the researchers have the place to themselves. They are generous hosts, and also, after a year alone, very glad of new faces at dinner.

Daylight there is dimmer than you expect and brighter than you fear. Ilyr is a brilliant point rather than a disc, and noon on Mirren is about as bright as a deep dusk on Calder: enough to walk by, enough to read by, never enough to warm anything. Inside, the station is warm, close and friendly, and everyone eats together at one long table.

Ice mountains, nitrogen plains and a sky of haze

The Hollin Range is made of water ice, frozen so hard at these temperatures that it behaves like rock. It holds cliffs, it forms ridges, it cracks into blocks the size of houses. The highest peaks reach about 3 km, and walking their lower slopes in a suit feels like any good mountain day, until you knock on a boulder and remember what it is made of.

Mirren does not look like a destination from there. It looks like a hole in the sky with a halo round it.

Below the mountains lie smooth plains of nitrogen ice, and they are the strangest ground I have ever stood on. Nitrogen ice is soft, as ices go. It flows, very slowly, and over long ages it has filled the low ground and levelled itself into pale fields that stretch to the horizon with barely a ripple. The guides keep visitors to the firm margins, and they are right to.

Above it all is the sky. Mirren's thin air holds layers of blue haze, a dozen or more stacked one above another, each a fine sheet of particles at its own height. At low sun they light up in bands, and the mountains stand against them in stark black and white, as the pictures in our gallery show. After a while you stop looking at the ground at all.

Leaving is the last gift. As the Swan pulls away and turns for home, Mirren slips between the ship and Ilyr, and the whole world becomes a thin dark disc with its haze glowing blue around the rim. Mirren does not look like a destination from there. It looks like a hole in the sky with a halo round it. Then, after a day or two, it looks like nothing at all. Most of us stayed at the windows until it was gone.

The Mirren expedition

  • Ship: the Long Swan, one sailing a year
  • Passage: about 40 days beyond Tessaly, itself 9 days from Halcyon on the standard transfer
  • Guests: 12, one for each guest berth at Hollin Station
  • Time at Hollin: a little under three weeks
  • Whole voyage: about 100 days from Tessaly and back
  • On the ground: the water-ice peaks of the Hollin Range, up to 3 km; smooth plains of nitrogen ice; layers of blue haze
  • Before you go: a suit course, and an hour's exercise every day on board

titles.en: The Blue Erg: a walker's guide to Orrin's dune seas

descriptions.en: Why Orrin's northern dunes are dark basalt that looks blue from orbit, how they creep a few metres a year, and how to walk them safely in a pressure suit.

bodies.en:
From orbit, the far north of Orrin carries a strange, cool stain across its red: the Blue Erg, a dune sea of dark sand that looks blue-grey in every picture taken from above. Down on it, in a suit, the sand looks almost black, the dunes rise in long, smooth curves, and the walking is some of the best in the Reach. Here is what you need to know before you go.

Why the sand is dark

Most of Orrin is red because it is coated in fine, iron-stained dust. The Erg is different because its sand is basalt: dark volcanic rock, broken down over long ages into grains about the size of table salt. Those grains are much heavier than the red dust. The wind can roll and bounce them along the ground, but it cannot lift them high and carry them off, so over time they have collected in the low northern plains while the fine dust blew on elsewhere.

Underfoot the sand is close to black, with a glitter of tiny greenish crystals when the sun is low. From orbit it reads as blue-grey, partly because of the pale ground between the dunes and partly because you are looking at it through dusty air, which scatters a little blue light of its own. The colour in the pictures is real, in other words, but you will not see it with your boots in it.

How the dunes move

The dunes are not fixed. The wind pushes grains up each dune's long, gentle windward slope and over the crest, where they tumble down the steep lee side, the slip face. Grain by grain, the whole dune walks downwind, a few metres a year. That is slow enough for a map to stay useful for years, and fast enough that the guide companies move their marker beacons every season.

Many of the Erg's dunes are crescents, with their two horns pointing downwind, and where several meet they merge into long, winding ridges.
