On their flanks and in the flats between them lie ripple fields: ridges a few centimetres high and a hand's width apart, their crests picked out in paler, coarser grains. Ripples are dunes in miniature, and they move far faster. Walk across a ripple field in the morning and your boot prints will be blurred by the afternoon.

Walking on dunes in a suit

Dune walking is tiring anywhere. In a pressure suit it asks for some technique, and your guide will teach it on the first morning. The essentials:

  1. Walk the windward side and the crests. Windward slopes are firm and gentle. Slip faces are steep, soft and inclined to slide, and a slide in a suit is hard to stop.
  2. Shorten your stride. Short, flat-footed steps waste less effort in soft sand than long ones, and keep your weight over your boots.
  3. Use poles. Two poles take some of the work off your legs and catch you when the sand gives way.
  4. Seal your boots. Basalt grains are hard and sharp, and they find their way into every joint. Fit the gaiters, check the ankle seals at every stop, and brush down thoroughly before you enter a hut lock.
  5. Drink by the clock. Suits are dry and the walking is warm work. Sip from your suit's water line every twenty minutes, thirsty or not.
  6. Watch your air. Hard walking uses more of it. Guides set the turn-back time by the slowest walker's supply, never the fastest.

The firmest ground in the Erg is the pale, cracked flats between the dunes, old dried-out hollows baked hard. When your legs are tired, aim for the pale ground. When the guide says no, it is usually because the crust over that particular hollow is thin.

Finding your way

The Erg is the easiest place on Orrin to get lost. Every dune looks like the last, there is no peak on the horizon to steer by, and blowing sand can cut visibility to a few hundred metres within the hour. The guide companies keep lines of marker beacons that show on your suit display, and every walker carries a locator. Learn to read the dunes as well: their slip faces all point the same way, downwind, and once you know which way that is you have a rough compass that keeps working when your display does not.

The rule is simple and absolute. Nobody walks the Erg alone, and nobody leaves the group, not even for a photograph from the next crest.

Guided crossings

Crossings start from Corran, from where a pressurised rover takes most of a day to reach the camp on the Erg's southern edge. The usual choice is between a two-day taster, out and back from the edge camp, and a five-day crossing, with the rover carrying a hut and supplies ahead to each night's stop. Groups are six at most, with a guide for every three walkers. Fitness matters more than experience: if you have walked the Gediz Rim trail, you will manage, and you will sleep very well.

Walking the Blue Erg

  • Getting to Orrin: 11 days from Halcyon on the standard crossing, 7 on the express
  • Where: Orrin's northern dune seas, most of a day by rover from Corran
  • Crossings: a two-day taster or a five-day crossing, groups of up to six
  • Sand: dark basalt, near-black underfoot, blue-grey from orbit
  • Dune speed: a few metres a year; ripples shift within hours
  • Bring: suit gaiters, two poles, a spare seal kit
  • Rules: never alone, never down a slip face, back by the turn-back time

titles.en: Kesh from the viewing approach

descriptions.en: Nobody lands on Kesh. From a shaded lounge behind a heat shield, a former hull inspector watches the furnace world's glowing night side and explains how the pass works.

bodies.en:
Nobody lands on Kesh. Nobody could: its day side is molten rock, and even its night side glows. The closest anyone gets is the viewing approach, a slow, shielded pass that a few liners make as special sailings from Halcyon, and it gave me the strangest few hours I have ever spent aboard a ship.

Why the liners slow down

Kesh is close to Ilyr, close enough that its surface melts, and it is tidally locked: one face always turned to the star, the other always turned away. A liner heading inward picks up speed as it falls towards Ilyr, and if it simply swept past, the planet would cross the windows in minutes. So on the approach the ship spends fuel to shed that speed, matching Kesh's pace as closely as she can, and holds at a safe distance for hours instead.

There is a second reason, and it is the one the engineers care about. Every hour that close to Ilyr is an hour of heat pouring onto the ship. Slowing down makes the pass predictable: the navigators can hold one attitude, the shield can face one direction, and the cooling plant can settle into a steady load rather than chasing a changing one. It is also why the viewing approach costs considerably more than other voyages of a similar length. You are paying for fuel spent on purpose, and for a shield that will need inspecting afterwards.

The shields

I spent nine years inspecting hulls at the Halcyon yards, and the ships back from Kesh were always the ones we lingered over. A viewing liner carries a heat shield across her sunward side, built in layers: a bright, reflective outer skin that turns most of Ilyr's light away, a ceramic layer behind it, a gap, and then a lattice of coolant lines that carries off whatever gets through. On the approach the ship turns that face to the star and keeps it there, and everything else, passengers included, lives in the shade behind it.

You can hear the shield at work. As the ship closes in, the hull ticks and creaks like a house in high summer, and the cooling pumps settle into a deep hum that you feel through the deck more than hear. That is normal. Back at Halcyon, every tile and coolant joint is checked before the ship sails again; I once pulled a cracked tile from a shield that looked perfect from the gallery.

During the approach every sunward window on the ship is shuttered and locked by the crew, and stays that way until the hull has cooled, about a day after the pass. Do not try to open one. It will not open, and the crew will want to know what you were doing.

The shaded lounges

The viewing happens in the shaded lounges, long rooms on the ship's shadow side with windows of heavily filtered glass. The ship is positioned so that those windows look past the edge of her own shield, across to Kesh. Sessions are booked in advance, in small groups, so the rooms never feel crowded. The lights are kept low, the chairs recline, and drinks are served cold, because the whole ship runs a few degrees warmer than usual for the length of the pass.

Book the session that covers the closest part of the approach if you can, and a later one as well. The view changes more than you expect, and the second time you will notice what you missed the first.

What you see

The night side

The face turned away from Ilyr is not dark. It glows a dull, deep red, the colour of embers that have nearly gone out. Across it run cracks and seams that glow brighter, where hotter rock lies close to the surface. For the first hour it is all you notice, and it is far more beautiful than anything that hot has a right to be.

The day side

The molten face is only ever seen at an angle, along the edge of the planet, and only through the heaviest filters. What you see is a rim of orange-white, crusting and breaking, with a faint haze of vapour above it. Beside it Ilyr blazes, cut down by the glass to a white disc you can bear to look at for a few seconds.

Between the two runs the boundary, where the day side's glare gives way to the night side's red, and that is where most people end up looking. Cameras struggle with the contrast, which is one reason the pictures you have seen of Kesh, ours included, tend to be artists' impressions rather than photographs.

It glows a dull, deep red, the colour of embers that have nearly gone out.

How long it lasts

The approach proper takes about three days: a day closing in, with the shutters coming down and the hull beginning to tick; about eight hours in the viewing position, the best two of them at the closest point; and a day pulling away. Then the shutters stay down for another day while the ship cools. On the way back to Halcyon the lounges are quiet, and the people in them tend to be looking at their own pictures, or, more often, at nothing in particular.

The viewing approach at a glance

  • Who sails it: a few liners, on special sailings from Halcyon
  • The approach: about three days, with eight hours in the viewing position
  • The best of it: the two hours at the closest point
  • Where you watch: the shaded lounges on the shadow side, booked in sessions
  • On board: sunward shutters locked from the approach until a day after the pass; the ship runs a little warm

It is a long way to go for eight hours. I have made the trip four times, and I would go again tomorrow.

titles.en: Interview: the keeper of the Brightwater observatory

descriptions.en: For eleven years Mira Calloway has kept the telescopes on Veyra's dark side. She talks about Lantern nights, the cold, and why the faint real thing beats the pictures.

bodies.en:
For eleven years Mira Calloway has kept the observatory at Brightwater, on the dark side of Tessaly's icy moon Veyra: three infrared telescopes on the ice, a viewing dome, a lodge of twelve rooms and the most talked-about nights in the outer Reach. We met in the lodge library, beneath a screen showing the Lantern in false colour, while the real one hung faint and grey beyond the window.

Calloway grew up on Calder's northern coast, where the aurora season is the event of the year, and trained as an instrument engineer before answering a notice for "a keeper, cold-tolerant, two years". She stayed for eleven. Our conversation has been edited for length.

The work

What does a keeper actually do?

Everything the astronomers would rather not think about. Brightwater is a working observatory first and a lodge second. The three big telescopes are infrared instruments, and an infrared telescope has to be cold, because anything warm glows in infrared, the telescope included. Veyra's dark side is one of the coldest places anyone works in the Reach, which is exactly why we are here. My job is to keep the instruments cold, clean and pointing where they should, and to keep the people who use them warm, fed and on speaking terms.

What does an ordinary shift look like?

The telescopes work through the dark, so the important hours are the ones the guests sleep through. I walk the field at the start of every shift, in a suit, checking the covers. Frost from the geysers at the south pole drifts round the moon and settles on everything as a fine white dust, so the covers are swept twice a shift. Then the cooling lines, the pumps, the supply manifest and the menu, which matters more than people think. Nine people in a small building a long way from anywhere will forgive almost anything except a bad week of dinners.

Who are the nine?

Two astronomers on rotation, two technicians, a cook, a doctor who is also our pilot, a walking guide, a housekeeper and me. A supply ship comes every few weeks. You learn to like the people you have.

Lantern nights

Brightwater is famous for its Lantern nights. What happens on one?

The telescopes are for work, so every second night we give the guests the dome. At eight by the lodge clock the lights go down to red, and from then until the small hours guests take turns at the dome telescope, the one instrument here built for human eyes. In the library we put up the infrared pictures the big telescopes took the night before, so you can stand between the two: the false colour on the screen, and the faint thing itself through the glass.

What do people actually see?

Less than they expect at first, and more than they expected by the end. To the naked eye the Lantern is a long pale smudge. Give your eyes half an hour in the dark and it grows edges. Through the dome telescope the Twin Fires resolve into two knots of stars, and once your eyes have settled you can follow the Wing away from them like smoke from a chimney. I always explain the pictures before anyone looks. Green is warm dust, red is the hottest glowing gas, blue is starlight. Our pictures are true, but they are not what your eye will ever see. The eye sees grey and a little silver, and that is enough.

Do guests feel cheated?

Almost never. Someone usually goes quiet at the eyepiece and stays far longer than their turn. In my first year I moved them on. Now I let them stay, and the queue nearly always agrees with me.

Our pictures are true, but they are not what your eye will ever see.

Do you have a favourite part of the Lantern?

The Nursery, where stars are still forming. In infrared it is full of bright knots, each one a young star still wrapped in the dust it is being made from. One of them was barely there when I arrived, and it is brighter every season. I have watched a star grow up, more or less, which is not something many people can say about their job.

Guests and the cold

Who comes all this way?

Fewer people than you might think, and more kinds. Retired liner crews who spent their working lives too busy to look out of the window. Couples. Students who saved for years. Once a family with three children under ten, who were among the best guests we have had: children adapt to the dark faster than adults and complain about the cold less.

How cold is it?

Outside, around two hundred degrees below freezing. Nobody meets that directly. You meet it through a suit, and the suits are very good. What guests feel is the dome, which we keep at ten below. Warm air rising past cold glass makes the stars swim, so a warm dome is a blurred dome. We hand out lodge parkas at the door, and mittens with a flap for one finger, for the focus knob.

And what does the cold do to you, after eleven years?

The cold is not the hard part. The hard part is the dark. Your body still wants a sun. We have a lamp room with a bright white panel, and everyone, me included, sits under it for twenty minutes at breakfast. There is also the hot room, a small sauna beside the laundry, where most of the lodge's arguments are settled. Nobody stays cross at that temperature for long.

What eleven years teach

What have you learned about the people who come?

That nearly everyone whispers in the dome, although there is nothing out there to disturb. That the guests who ask the most questions on the first night ask none on the third. And that people come for the pictures and go home talking about the dark. On Calder there is always a town on the horizon, or Selka, or the aurora. Here there is nothing between you and the Lantern but glass.

Will you stay?

I tell myself every renewal is the last. Then a supply ship comes in, somebody new climbs into the dome on their first Lantern night and goes completely silent, and I sign again.

Brightwater in brief

  • Where: Veyra's dark side. Tessaly is 9 days from Halcyon on the standard transfer; the shuttle from orbit lands beside the lodge.
  • The lodge: twelve rooms, a library, a lamp room and a hot room, with a staff of nine.
  • Lantern nights: every second night, from eight by the lodge clock. A stay of six nights gives you three.
  • The dome: kept at ten degrees below freezing; parkas and mittens are lent at the door.

titles.en: Choosing a cabin: windows, spin and noise

descriptions.en: Which ring, which side, which wall? A former hull inspector on choosing a berth on a liner or on Halcyon, and on which upgrades are worth your marks.

bodies.en:
For nine years I inspected hulls at the Halcyon yards, which means I have been inside more liner cabins than most stewards, usually behind the panels with a torch. Here is what that taught me about where to sleep: which ring, which side of the ship, and which wall you do not want your bed against.

Spin: the ring decides your weight

A liner makes weight the only way it can, by spinning. Cabins sit on rings that turn round the ship's long axis, and the floor presses up on you because it is constantly being swung round. The further a cabin is from the centre, the faster its floor moves and the heavier you feel. That is the whole of the physics, and it governs most of what follows.

Spin has a second effect that brochures leave out. In a turning room, anything that moves towards or away from the centre is nudged sideways, so a jug pours in a slight curve and standing up quickly can bring a brief, seasick lurch. The nudge is the same on both rings of a ship, but the inner ring gives you less weight to steady yourself against, so there it feels much stronger. Most people stop noticing within two days. Light sleepers notice it every time they roll over.

Outer ring

Noticeably more weight. Water stays in the cup, showers drain properly, and most people sleep more deeply.

  • Usually adds a tenth to a sixth to the fare
  • The sideways lurch is mild
  • The ring to book for any crossing longer than a few days

Inner ring

Lighter, cheaper and, for some, a pleasure: people with sore knees or backs often swear by it, and children love it.

  • The sideways lurch is stronger
  • Showers are slow and spilled tea travels
  • Often the cheapest berths aboard

Windows: sunward or shadow side

Cabin windows are on one side of the ring or the other: sunward, towards Ilyr, or shadow side, away from it. Liners hold the same attitude for most of a crossing, because their shields and radiators are built that way round, so the side you book is the side you get from dock to dock.

Sunward windows are bright, warm and shuttered for much of the day, since Ilyr's glare through an open pane is not something you sit in for long. What they offer is the Reach backlit: on the approach to Tessaly, the rings lit into a halo; around Veyra, the geyser plumes glittering. Shadow-side windows look into the dark. The stars move steadily across the pane as the ring turns, which takes a few minutes to get used to and then becomes the best screen aboard, and the worlds you pass appear lit full face. Further out, the Lantern rises in them. They are also darker for sleeping and a degree or two cooler.

Noise: the drive, the spokes and the galley

Cabins near the drive section, at the stern, have a reputation, and on departure day they earn it: during a burn the drive's hum comes through the hull as a note you feel in your teeth. But a transfer is mostly a long coast. The big burns come at the start and the end, with a few short corrections in between, and for the rest of the crossing an aft cabin is as quiet as any. Aft berths are often priced as if the drive ran all the time. It does not.

The quietest berth on a liner is rarely the most expensive one.

The noises that last all crossing are elsewhere. Where a ring's spokes meet the hub there are bearings, and a cabin beside a spoke hears their low rumble carried down through the floor, along with the lift in the spoke itself, which runs all night. The air and water plant has pumps that cycle every few minutes. The galley starts work hours before breakfast. And a cabin under the gym or beside the bar has its own obvious problem.

For light sleepers. Ask for a cabin mid-way between two spokes, on the outer ring and the shadow side, and nowhere near the galley. Ask by deck plan rather than by cabin grade: two cabins of the same grade can be a world apart in comfort, and the purser can see which is which.

On Halcyon

The same rules hold on Halcyon Station, only gentler. The wheel is 2.4 km across and turns once every 70 seconds, slowly enough that the lurch is barely there on the Rim deck, which gives you nearly your full Calder weight. Rooms on the outer ring are the ones to book: people sleep better in them, and after a liner's lighter rings you will feel the difference on the first night. Expect to pay from about 260 marks a night on the Rim deck and from about 150 on the inner rings, which are lighter, cheaper and perfectly good for a nap between connections.

A window room costs about a third more. For one night, skip it: the window cafés along the Promenade cost the price of a pot of tea. Rooms beside the dock spokes hear the clamps whenever a liner comes in or leaves, so ask for one away from them.

What is worth paying for

After nine years behind the panels, this is my order of spending, most worthwhile first.

  1. The outer ring. Weight is sleep, and sleep is the difference between arriving and recovering.
  2. A shadow-side window on a long crossing. On nine days to Tessaly or eleven to Orrin, it is the view you will live with. On the two days to Selka, it hardly matters.
  3. A berth between spokes. Often free, if you ask early.
  4. A sunward window, only for an arrival you care about. If the rings or the geysers are the point of the trip, it earns its price on the last day.
  5. Not worth it: paying to be far from the drive. An aft cabin is quiet for most of the crossing, and its discount is one of the few real bargains aboard.

The quietest berth on a liner is rarely the most expensive one. It is the one somebody chose with a deck plan in hand.

titles.en: Aster opens its first island permits

descriptions.en: The ocean world has opened its Sunward Chain to visitors for the first time: 2,000 permits a year, drawn by ballot. How to apply, and what the islanders ask in return.

bodies.en:
For as long as liners have crossed the Reach, Aster has been a world you looked at and did not visit: a blue globe in a wrap of white cloud, its islands strung across the ocean in long, broken lines. That has changed. The islanders of the Sunward Chain have opened their first permits for visitors, two thousand a year and no more, and the first applications are already in.

What has been announced

The permits were approved by the Chain's island council after what one councillor described to us as "a long argument, conducted politely". The quota is fixed at 2,000 visitors a year, counted per person, children included. Stays are capped at twelve days. Visitors will land on Tarrow, the largest island and the only one with a landing field, and may travel by island boat to two neighbours, Sorrel and Quill. The rest of the Chain stays closed.

Nobody is building hotels. Every visitor will stay in an island house, in a guest room let by a family who have agreed to take visitors, with meals at the family table. The council says around ninety households have signed up so far, which is why the quota is what it is.

The reasons for opening, as the islanders put them, are practical. The permit fees will pay for a new desalination plant and a harbour wall on Tarrow. Younger islanders want work that does not mean leaving. And, as the councillor said, "if the Reach is going to come and look at us, we would rather it came to the door."

How to apply

Applications go through the council's permit office on Halcyon Station, in person or by message, during a thirty-day window that opens with each quota year. There is no queue to join and no advantage in applying early: permits are drawn by ballot once the window closes.

  1. Apply as a group of up to four. A group is drawn together or not at all.
  2. Pay the application fee of 40 marks a person. It is not refunded, whatever the draw.
  3. Write a short statement of why you want to come. The council says it reads every one and scores none.
  4. Wait for the draw. Results are promised within sixty days of the window closing.
  5. If drawn, pay the permit fee of 1,500 marks a person within thirty days, and choose your dates. Most of it goes into the islands' water and harbour fund.

Permits are named and cannot be sold or passed on. Places that are not taken up go back into a second, smaller draw.

What the islanders ask

The council has published a short list of requests. The islanders we spoke to were clear that they are requests in name only.

  • Water is rain. Every drop on the Chain is caught from the roofs, and a visitor's share is 60 litres a day. Showers are short; laundry is done by the household.
  • The boats are the islanders'. No private craft, and no hired boat without an island skipper.
  • Take nothing from the shore or the sea: no shells, no stones, and no fishing except with your hosts.
  • Keep the rest day. One day in seven the boats stay in, the shops close and the islands go quiet. Visitors are asked to go quiet too.
  • Ask before you photograph anyone, and leave flying cameras at home: they are not allowed.

"We are not opening a resort," said Hana Rell, who will host visitors in two rooms of her house on Tarrow. "We are opening our doors. People who understand the difference will be very happy here."

What we know so far

Very little has been written about the islands by outsiders, and much of what follows comes from the council's own notes. The Chain lies near the equator and is warm all year, with rain most afternoons and a stormy season the islanders call the long blow, when the boats stay in for days at a time and no visitors are received. The islands are low and green, and none takes more than a few hours to walk from end to end. Food is fish, seaweed, root crops and bread, and the islanders are proud of their bread.

Questions remain. The council has not yet named the crossings that permit holders will travel on, nor said whether the quota will grow if the first year goes well. Asked about that, the councillor smiled and said the islands would decide once they had met us. We will report from Tarrow as soon as we have been.

Aster permits at a glance

  • Quota: 2,000 visitors a year, children included
  • The draw: by ballot, after a thirty-day application window
  • Fees: 40 marks a person to apply; 1,500 marks a person if drawn
  • Stay: up to 12 days, in island houses only
  • Open islands: Tarrow, Sorrel and Quill
  • Water: 60 litres a person a day

titles.en: Stargazing from Veyra's dark side: a beginner's map of the Lantern

descriptions.en: Where to start, what to look for and how to train your eyes: a first-night route round the Lantern's regions from Brightwater, from the Twin Fires to the faint Veil.

bodies.en:
The first time you see the Lantern from Veyra you may wonder, for a minute or two, what the fuss is about. It is fainter than the pictures and greyer than the posters, a pale cloud across the dark. Then your eyes catch up. This is a map for that first night: where to begin, what to look for, and how to get your eyes to do more than you thought they could.

First, give your eyes the dark

Your pupils open within a minute of the lights going out, but that is the least of it. The real change happens in the eye's chemistry, and it takes about half an hour. A single glance at a white screen undoes most of it, which is why the lodge at Brightwater goes over to red light at eight by the lodge clock on Lantern nights, and why the staff will ask, politely and then less politely, for screens to stay in pockets.

The dome is kept at ten degrees below freezing, because warm air rising past cold glass makes the stars swim. Dress for it. The lodge lends parkas and mittens with a flap for one finger, but your own warm socks and a hat make the difference between an hour at the eyepiece and twenty minutes.

Look away to see more. The centre of your eye is built for detail in good light; its edges are better in the dark. To see a faint cloud, look a little to one side of it. It feels like cheating. It works.

A map in five steps

The Lantern is large, so learn it the way you would learn a city: one landmark first, then the streets that lead from it. Start bright and work towards faint.

  1. The Twin Fires. Begin with the brightest part of the Lantern, two hazy points side by side, close enough that one thumb held at arm's length covers both. Each is a cluster of young, hot stars. Everything else on this map is found from here.
  2. The Wing. From the Twin Fires a long, faint streamer runs away across the sky, like a feather laid on black cloth. In Brightwater's infrared pictures it is a long green cloud of warm dust with a bright red head: gas, nearest the clusters, heated by them until it glows.
  3. The Reef. On the other side of the Fires lies a mottled patch, lumpy rather than smooth. In false colour it is the busiest part of the Lantern: blue where starlight shines through, red where gas glows, and orange where glowing gas and warm dust overlap.
  4. The Nursery. Below the Reef, look for a few soft knots that refuse to sharpen however carefully you focus. They are young stars still forming, wrapped in the dust they are made from, and they are the dome telescope's best target.
  5. The Witch, the Butterfly and the Veil. These take patience. The Witch is a hooked profile of warm dust at the Lantern's edge, far easier to see once someone has traced it for you. The Butterfly is two small lobes of glowing gas, a telescope object. The Veil is the faint sheet that frames all of it, and it is usually the last thing a new eye finds, often well into the first hour.

Binoculars or telescope?

Brightwater keeps both, and the order in which you use them matters: eyes first, then binoculars, then the telescope.

Binoculars

The beginner's best friend. A pair of seven- or ten-power binoculars shows the Lantern's shapes whole: the Wing from end to end, the lumps of the Reef, the Witch's nose. Brace them on the dome rail and the view steadies.

  • A wide view, so you keep your bearings
  • Easy to pass along a row
  • Lent by the lodge; bring your own if you have them

The dome telescope

It shows what binoculars cannot: the Twin Fires breaking into separate stars, the knots of the Nursery, the two wings of the Butterfly. The view is narrow, so the shapes are lost, and the queue means a few minutes at a time.

  • A narrow view: know where you are first
  • Best for the Nursery and the Butterfly
  • The staff point it; you focus
The Lantern rewards patience more than equipment.

On the last night of most stays the guides lead a short suit walk out to the telescope field, and the Lantern overhead through a visor, with no dome between you and it, is a different thing. Leave the binoculars behind, because they do not work against a helmet. Switch to the clear night visor before you go out, and give your eyes a few minutes to settle again once you are outside.

Lantern nights at Brightwater

Brightwater is a working observatory, and on most nights its three infrared telescopes have the dark to themselves. Every second night the dome belongs to the guests. A staff astronomer gives a short tour of the sky with a dim red pointer, the dome telescope is set on each region in turn, and in the library the infrared pictures from the night before are on the screens, so you can set the false colour beside the faint grey original. Remember the key: green for warm dust, red for the hottest glowing gas, blue for starlight.

Plan for three Lantern nights, which means a stay of six. On the first your eyes are learning. By the third you will find the Wing without help, and you will understand why the people around you have stopped talking. The Lantern rewards patience more than equipment.

Before your first Lantern night

  • Allow half an hour of darkness before you judge what you can see.
  • Red light only; screens stay in your room.
  • Dress for ten degrees below freezing: a hat, warm socks, layers.
  • Start with the Twin Fires, then the Wing, then the Reef.
  • Use binoculars before the telescope.

titles.en: Veyra's Glass Shore: what the first visitors found

descriptions.en: Liora Venn joined one of the first small groups allowed into Veyra's ice cavern: a slow descent, a lake beneath clear ice, cliffs full of light and a silence nobody wanted to break.

bodies.en:
There were six of us and two guides, and for the first hour nobody said much beyond the checks: seals, air, radio, line. We were one of the first small groups allowed into the cavern on Veyra that people have started calling the Glass Shore, and none of us knew quite what to expect, except that it would be cold and that we would not be allowed to touch anything.

The descent

The cavern opens in a low ice cliff, its mouth turned towards Ilyr. From the landing pad it is a two-hour ride by crawler across a plain of frozen ridges, with the sun low on the horizon the whole way and the shadows of the ridges stretched out for hundreds of metres beside us.

Veyra's gravity is so slight that the way down is less a climb than a slow, guided fall. We clipped to a fixed line and let ourselves down a ramp of ice some eighty metres long, hand over hand, boots barely touching. Our lead guide, Petra Voss, had been down it more than forty times. She went first and talked the whole way, in the calm, unhurried voice of someone reading out the shipping forecast. At the bottom the ramp levels onto a broad shelf, and the cavern opens around you. That is the moment every account of the Glass Shore tries to describe, and I am about to fail in the same way.

The light

Ilyr was just above the horizon behind us, and its light came in through the cavern mouth almost level, along the floor and up into the walls. The walls are ice cliffs thirty or forty metres high, and they are clear. Not white, as ice is everywhere else on Veyra, but clear, so that light goes into them and comes back out somewhere else, bent and softened. Petra explained that this ice froze very slowly from meltwater, with no bubbles to scatter the light, and that this is why visitors say it looks like glass. Knowing why did not help in the slightest.

Where the light struck the cliffs head on they glowed pale gold. Further in, where it had passed through more ice, it turned blue, then a deep, inky blue-green, and at the back of the cavern it ran out altogether. Our lamps were set to their lowest. We were asked to keep them that way, and nobody argued.

The lake

The lake lies along the foot of the cliffs, black and perfectly still. It is liquid water, warmed from below by the same heat inside Veyra that drives the geysers at the south pole, and it is roofed by a skin of clear ice a few centimetres thick. From the shelf it looks like a hole in the floor. Petra knelt at the marked edge and angled her lamp down, and through the skin we could see the water moving: slow currents, a few pale specks of frost turning over in them.

Someone asked how deep it was. Nobody knows. The first survey team lowered a weighted line two hundred metres and found no bottom, and that line is still the only thing that has been in the water. The rules are written to keep it that way.

The silence

Sound does not travel through a vacuum, so in one sense a suit is always silent. In practice it is noisy: the fans, your own breathing, the click of the radio, six people saying "look at that" at once. At the shore Petra called a minute of radio quiet. One by one we switched off. For the first time since the shuttle, nobody said a word.

A minute became five. I listened to my breathing slow. Across the lake the cliffs went on glowing, gold at the front and blue at the back, and the light shifted on the walls as Ilyr crept along the horizon outside. When the radio came back on, the first thing anyone said, after a long pause, was a quiet "thank you", and it was not clear to whom.

For the first time since the shuttle, nobody said a word.

The rules that protect it

Visits to the Glass Shore are deliberately small and deliberately few, and the rules are read out at the landing pad and again on the shelf.

  • Six visitors, two guides, never more.
  • Stay on the line. A cord on the ice marks where you may walk; the lake's edge is a metre beyond it.
  • Touch nothing. A suit glove is warmer than the ice and leaves a mark that lasts for years.
  • Lamps on low, and no flash. The light is the point.
  • Forty minutes at the shore, then back up the line.
  • Nothing taken, nothing left.

It is a short list, and on the way back up the ramp it seemed a small price. The Glass Shore has been open to visitors for less than a season. If it is to look to the next groups the way it looked to us, the line on the ice will have to hold.

Visiting the Glass Shore

  • Groups: six visitors and two guides
  • Getting there: two hours by crawler from the landing pad, then an 80-metre descent on a fixed line
  • Time at the shore: forty minutes
  • Fitness: you need to be comfortable in a suit for about four hours; no climbing experience is required
  • Combine it with: a stay at Brightwater and a guided walk to the geysers

titles.en: What the new transfer timetable means for travellers

descriptions.en: Windows to Tessaly still open every 26 days, but each now carries an express, and the equinox season gets crossings of its own. What changes for fares, and how to plan.

bodies.en:
The Halcyon transfer office has published its timetable for the next twelve windows to the outer Reach, and for once the small print repays a careful read. The windows themselves have not moved, because they cannot. Almost everything around them has.

What has not changed

Liners to Tessaly still leave in windows that open every 26 days, when the positions of Calder and Tessaly let a ship fall outward around Ilyr on a transfer orbit that saves fuel. That rhythm is set by the worlds, not by the timetable, and no schedule will change it. Each window stays open for about four days. The standard crossing still takes nine. Miss a window and the next one is 26 days away, which is the single most important fact in this article.

The Morning Lark keeps its own long loop of 14 days, outside the transfer timetable, and remains the choice for anyone who wants a slow voyage rather than an efficient one.

What is new

Three changes matter.

  1. An express in every window. Until now the express to Tessaly ran in every other window, so half the year's travellers had no fast option at all. From the first window of the new timetable each one carries an express, leaving on the window's last day and arriving in six days rather than nine.
  2. Standard departures spread out. Each window used to send both its standard liners out on the opening day. They will now leave two days apart, which eases the crush at the Halcyon gates and gives anyone who misses the first a second chance inside the same window.
  3. Equinox crossings. Four windows around Tessaly's coming equinox are marked as equinox crossings, with an extra standard sailing in each.

The equinox season

At Tessaly's equinox the rings go edge-on to Ilyr, and for a while they all but vanish: their shadow on the planet shrinks to a thin dark line, and the shadows of the moons can be seen crossing the cloud tops. It is one of the rarest views in the Reach, and the giant's long year means most people will get one chance at it. The transfer office expects demand to run well ahead of seats, which is why it has added sailings rather than simply raising the price of the existing ones.

Arrive in the equinox season and the rings are the obvious draw, but they are not the only one. With the rings narrowed to a line, Veyra and Thule stand out clearly against the planet, and the view of the Rose at the north pole, with no ring shadow anywhere near it, is as clean as it ever gets.

What it does to fares

Standard fares are unchanged, from about 3,600 marks one way in an inner-ring cabin. Express fares fall slightly, from about 9,600 marks to 8,900, because there are now twice as many seats to sell. Equinox crossings carry a supplement of up to a fifth on every class of berth, and it applies to the four marked windows only.

The quiet bargain. The windows just before and just after the equinox crossings are sold at ordinary fares, and the rings narrow for weeks either side of the equinox itself, so they will still be a thin bright line when you arrive. If the view is the point of your trip and the supplement is not, book one of those.

How to plan now

  1. Book three windows ahead. Sales open 78 days before departure, and the equinox crossings are expected to sell out within days.
  2. Build in a spare day at Halcyon. The shuttle from Port Kestrel takes about 6 hours. Arriving the day before your liner costs a night on the Rim deck, from about 260 marks; a missed departure can cost 26 days.
  3. Choose your speed by the calendar, not only the fare. The express saves three days each way, which on a short leave is the difference between a week at Veyra and four days.
  4. Check the way home first. Return windows run on the same 26-day rhythm, so the length of your stay at Tessaly is set by the windows home, not by your wishes.

None of this makes the outer Reach cheap, and nothing will. But for the first time the timetable is built around the people on it, and anyone planning a crossing in the next year should read it before they book anything else.

The new timetable at a glance

  • Windows to Tessaly: every 26 days, each open for about four days
  • Standard crossing: 9 days; two liners a window, two days apart
  • Express: 6 days; now in every window, not every other
  • Equinox crossings: four windows, an extra standard sailing in each, a supplement of up to a fifth
  • Fares, one way: standard from about 3,600 marks; express from about 8,900
  • Booking: opens 78 days before departure

titles.en: Forty-eight hours on Halcyon Station

descriptions.en: Most travellers only change ships at Halcyon. Stay two days instead: walk the Promenade, tour the violet-lit gardens and the shipyards, and end at the Long Window at dusk.

bodies.en:
Most people treat Halcyon Station the way you treat a corridor: off the shuttle from Port Kestrel, a cup of something at the gate, onto the liner and away. That is a mistake. The great wheel over Calder is a small city with a long street, its own farms, a shipyard and the best window in the Reach, and two days is just about enough to do it properly.

Day one: the Promenade

The shuttle takes about six hours from Port Kestrel: a few minutes pressed into your seat at three times your weight, then weightless all the way to docking. You arrive at the hub, where you still float, and ride a spoke lift down towards the rim. Weight comes back gently on the way, and by the time the doors open on the Rim deck you have nearly all of it. The wheel is 2.4 km across and turns once every 70 seconds, slowly enough that you barely notice, unless you turn your head quickly in the lift.

Drop your bag and go straight to the Promenade, the long curved street that runs round the Rim deck. The odd thing about it, and the thing you will remember, is that the floor rises ahead of you in both directions, so that you always seem to be at the bottom of a valley that walks along with you. There are chandlers, a barber, tailors who alter suits, and a bakery that opens at five for the dock crews. A brisk walk takes you round the whole ring in under an hour. Walk on and you arrive where you began, which is the whole joke of the place.

Day one: window cafés and the gardens

Halcyon's window cafés are its living rooms: narrow places along the Promenade with a strip of window, where you can sit for an hour over one pot of tea and watch Calder below. Some have windows set in the floor, through which the planet swings past once every turn of the wheel; first-timers tend to prefer a table by the wall. The best seats face Calder's limb, the thin bright line where the air meets the dark. Go mid-morning, when the crews have gone back to work.

Walk on and you arrive where you began, which is the whole joke of the place.

Have lunch there too, because the hydroponic gardens close for an hour at noon. Go down in the early afternoon. They are on the lower deck, beneath the Promenade, and they grow most of the station's vegetables in long racks under violet light, which makes the leaves look nearly black and your hands look bruised. It is warm and damp and smells of wet soil, the only place on the station that does. Visitors keep to the central walk; the gardeners will tell you which racks are being picked and, if you ask nicely, let you try a pea pod.

Dinner is back on the Promenade, and then bed. Book a room on the outer ring, from about 260 marks a night: with nearly full weight people sleep better there than anywhere else on the station, and after a day of walking you will.

Day two: the shipyards and the departures gallery

Halcyon's shipyards build and repair most of the liners in the Reach, and the morning tour is the best value on the station. Bring identification and wear closed shoes; you will be turned away without either. You will see hull sections longer than a row of Promenade cafés, welders at work in the weightless bays at the hub, and a liner's ring being balanced, which is slower and more delicate than you would think. Our ships editor, Tomas Arkwright, spent nine years here inspecting hulls. He says the guides are good, and that the best questions are about the welds.

Tour tips. Book a day ahead at the yard office on the Promenade. Tours run in the morning and last about two hours, including the weightless bays, so eat a light breakfast.

In the afternoon, go to the departures gallery and watch a liner leave. The gallery sits over the dock, with windows in its floor, and when the clamps let go the ship does not so much leave as fall away beneath your feet, dropping back and out of sight as the wheel turns on without it. The boards list every sailing. The gallery is busiest in a Tessaly window, when families come to wave.

Dusk at the Long Window

End at the Long Window, Halcyon's observation deck, reopened after its refit: a curved window 300 metres long, with a darkened deck and benches along its length. The dawn sessions are the ones to plan for: bookings open three days ahead, and the best dawns go within hours. Dusk, the hour when the station's orbit carries it into Calder's shadow, is easier to walk into and, to my mind, better. You watch the day side slide away and the limb thin to a line of blue, and then comes the night side, dark but for the towns. In the aurora season a band of green light hangs over the pole. If the timing is right, Selka rises at the end of the window, grey and sharp-edged.

Keep your voice down and your flash off: the deck has quiet hours, and the staff enforce them kindly but firmly. Then walk back along the Promenade to your room, and in the morning board your liner like someone who has actually been to Halcyon.

Halcyon in two days: the essentials

  • Getting there: about 6 hours by shuttle from Port Kestrel
  • Rooms: outer ring from about 260 marks a night; inner rings from about 150
  • Gardens: on the lower deck; closed for an hour at noon
  • Shipyard tours: mornings; bring identification and closed shoes; book a day ahead
  • Long Window: dawn sessions book up; dusk is usually walk-in; no flash
  • Weight: nearly full on the Rim deck, lighter on the inner rings; turn your head slowly in the lifts

titles.en: Why the stars do not twinkle in space

descriptions.en: Twinkling is the air's doing. Above it, stars are steady points in true colours, which changes how you look on Selka and Veyra, and explains why pictures of bright planets show no stars.

bodies.en:
Every child on Calder learns that stars twinkle. Most travellers find out, on their first night aboard a liner or on Halcyon Station, that they do not. The stars outside the window are steady, hard little points, so still that some people find them unsettling, as if someone had painted them on. Nothing is wrong with the stars. What has gone is the air.

Twinkling is the air's doing

Calder's atmosphere is not one clear layer but a restless stack of them, warmer and cooler pockets of air sliding past one another, each bending light very slightly differently. A star is so far away that its light reaches you as a single, impossibly thin thread. Every pocket of air that drifts across that thread pushes it about, a little brighter, a little dimmer, a little to one side, many times a second. That flicker is twinkling.

Near the horizon, where starlight crosses far more air, the effect is strongest, and a bright star low in the sky can flash red, white and blue as the air splits its light and puts it back together. On a windy night the stars twinkle more, on a still one less. Planets, by contrast, barely twinkle at all. A planet is close enough to show a tiny disc, so its light arrives as a bundle of threads, and the jostling averages out across them. Hence the old navigators' rule on Calder: if it twinkles, it is a star.

Steady points, true colours

Above the atmosphere there is nothing to jostle the thread, and a star simply shines. Two things follow, and both surprise people. The first is that there are far more stars than you expected, because the faint ones are no longer smeared out by the air or lost in its glow. The second is colour. Through Calder's air most stars look white. Above it the brighter ones show their colours plainly: some are orange, a few a deep amber-red, the hottest a cold blue-white. Ilyr itself, which sinks gold and orange into the sea at sunset, is a fierce yellow-white seen from orbit.

There is one exception, and it is worth knowing. A liner's cabin is warm and its window is cold, and the thin layer of air moving against the inside of the glass can make the stars shimmer slightly, as if a little of Calder's weather had come along for the ride. The only place a star twinkles in space is inside your own window. That is also why Brightwater, the observatory on Veyra, keeps its viewing dome at ten degrees below freezing: a warm dome is a blurred one.

Try it in your cabin. Turn the heating down and the lights off for half an hour before you look, and keep your breath off the glass. If the pane feels much colder than the room, expect a little shimmer; give it time and it settles.

The only place a star twinkles in space is inside your own window.

What it means on Selka and Veyra

On an airless world the stars behave as they do from orbit, all the way down to the horizon. On Selka they set as steady points, snuffed out by the edge of a grey hill rather than reddening and flickering into it as they would on Calder. The sky is black by day, but the sunlit ground is so bright that your pupils close down and only the brightest stars show. Stand in a deep shadow (the shadow of the Sixth Station boulder is the classic one), shade your visor from the glare and wait. After a few minutes, stars come out at midday.

Veyra's dark side is better still, since there is no sunlit ground to fight. Two practical points apply on both moons. First, switch to your suit's clear night visor: the tinted day visor that protects your eyes in sunlight cuts out the faint stars too. Second, binoculars and helmets do not mix, so for anything faint do your looking from inside a dome. Outside, enjoy the stars as they are: steady, sharp and in colour. Orrin, with its thin, cold air, sits in between. Its stars twinkle, but lazily.

Why the pictures leave out the stars

People often ask why photographs of Tessaly, or of Calder from Halcyon, show a sky with no stars in it. Nobody has removed them. A sunlit world is enormously brighter than any star behind it, and a camera set to show a planet's clouds properly gives the stars far too little light to register. Set the camera for the stars and the planet becomes a white blank. Your eyes do much the same: on the sunlit side of the station, looking at Calder, you will see no stars at all.

So when you see a picture of a bright planet hanging in a sky full of stars, it is almost always two exposures combined, or a painting, and the better photographers say so in the caption. The pictures of the Lantern from Brightwater, like the Witch, are crowded with stars for the opposite reason: nothing bright is in the frame, and the telescope can gather the faint light for as long as it likes.

descriptions.en: A travel magazine for the Reach: its worlds, its stations and its ships.

bodies.en:
{name} is a travel magazine for the Reach: the worlds, stations and ships between Ilyr and the edge, and the people who cross between them. We write the stories we want to read before a crossing, and the guides we wish we had read after one.

What we cover

Destinations, from the grey hills of Selka to the ice mountains of Mirren. The stations and ports where journeys change ships. The liners themselves, slow and fast. Practical guides, with prices in marks and the hours things close. And the sky: the Lantern, the aurora, and the reasons things out here look the way they do.

We write the stories we want to read before a crossing.

Who we are

Liora Venn

Destinations editor. Has crossed the Reach eleven times and still books the window seat.

Tomas Arkwright

Ships and journeys. Nine years inspecting hulls at the Halcyon yards.

Ilse Marrow

Science correspondent, and a planetary geologist by training.

Dev Castellan

Practical travel. Once ran a hostel next to the Port Kestrel launch pads.

Saskia Imre

Night-sky editor, on more observatory decks than she can count.

Our pictures

The photographs in {name} are real. They were made by NASA: by its Cassini, Curiosity, New Horizons and Spitzer missions, and by astronauts in orbit. Here they are captioned as the places of the Reach, and every caption carries its credit. The few paintings among them are artist's impressions, and their captions say so.

titles.en: Aurelian Lines: the equinox crossing

descriptions.en: Nine nights to Tessaly, timed for the shadow line. An advertisement.

bodies.en:
Nine nights across the Reach, timed so that you arrive as Tessaly's rings turn edge-on. Aurelian Lines has sailed to Tessaly since the first regular crossings, and this season every Aurelian liner carries a gallery built for one view.

The equinox crossing

Four times a year the rings of Tessaly line up with Ilyr, and their shadow shrinks to a single line across the planet. Our equinox sailings leave Halcyon so that the last night of the crossing falls in that week. You spend it in the Aurelian Gallery, a curved lounge of windows on the shadow side, with the lights down and the galley open until the shadow passes.

Standard crossing

Nine nights, Halcyon to Tessaly, outer-ring cabin with a window. From 3,900 marks.

Equinox crossing

Nine nights, timed for the shadow line, with a reserved seat in the Gallery. From 4,600 marks.

On board

Every cabin is on the outer ring, where the weight is nearly full and people sleep. The galley cooks for eighty, not eight hundred. There is a library, a quiet deck with no announcements, and a doctor who has crossed more often than the captain.

Included

  • Outer-ring cabin with a window
  • All meals in the galley
  • A seat in the Aurelian Gallery on the equinox night
  • Transfer to the Veyra shuttle at Tessaly

A pressure suit is the one piece of luggage you live inside. Kestrel & Vane have fitted them in Port Kestrel for three generations, one traveller at a time.

Fitted, not sized

Rental suits come in sizes; people do not. We measure you in forty places, fit the joints to how you actually walk, and set the visor to your eyes. A suit made this way weighs less on a long day, and you stop noticing it by the second.

For every world

The Rim

For Orrin's trails: dust seals at every joint, a sun visor for the blue hour, and boots that grip sand ridges.

The Shelter

For Veyra and Selka: warm to two hundred below, and lights for walking in the dark.

The fitting

  • Two visits, ten days apart
  • At our workshop in the Old Docks, Port Kestrel
  • From 1,200 marks, with a year of free adjustments

bodies.en:
Eighteen rooms on the rim of the Gediz canyon, an hour's walk from Corran, every one of them facing the drop.

Wake up above the Gediz

Rimstone Lodge is built into the canyon wall, pressurised and warm, with windows that run from floor to ceiling. Walkers on the Gediz Rim trail stay on their first or last night; others come for a week and never put on a suit.

Every room faces the drop.

The blue hour terrace

At dusk the lodge dims its lights and opens the terrace dome, and guests watch Ilyr set into the blue glow over the far rim. Our kitchen serves dinner after the sun has gone, when everyone is ready to talk again.

Staying

  • Rooms from 340 marks a night, with breakfast
  • A rover meets every arrival in Corran
  • Trail walkers: we keep your bags while you walk

Small groups, dark skies and guides who know the sky by heart. Nightglass Tours takes you to see the Lantern from Veyra and the aurora over Calder, with your own eyes.

Lantern nights on Veyra

Six nights on Veyra's dark side, three of them under the Lantern with a guide and a telescope. Your eyes adapt over the first hour, and the shapes come out one after another: the Twin Fires, the Wing, the Reef.

Aurora flights over Calder

From Port Kestrel during the season: twelve hours there and back, two of them under the arc, in an aircraft that dims every light in the cabin.

titles.en: Red world, grey moon

editorials.en:
This issue walks. Four days along the Gediz Rim, two across the Blue Erg, three in the grey hills of Selka: the Reach is best seen at walking pace, even when walking means a pressure suit and a hut every ten kilometres.

Dev Castellan wrote the guides he wishes his guests had read, Ilse Marrow explains why Orrin's sunsets turn blue, and Liora Venn found the window on Halcyon worth the queue. Pack light.

titles.en: The outer worlds

editorials.en:
Past Orrin the crossings get longer and the welcomes smaller. This issue goes out to the edge: to Veyra's geysers and its Glass Shore, to Thule, which almost nobody visits, and forty days further to the ice mountains of Mirren.

Saskia Imre maps the Lantern for beginners and talks to the keeper of Brightwater, Tomas Arkwright watches Kesh from behind a heat shield, and Ilse Marrow chases the Rose. Bring something warm.
